After 60+ hours, I still find Civilization VII surprisingly difficult to judge. That probably says more about the game than any simple positive or negative rating could.

There are things here I genuinely prefer over Civilization VI. Cities and towns can feel more organic, trade routes and resources form an actual network, and the Commander system makes warfare much more enjoyable to manage. Combat is probably my favourite part of the game. I also like the idea of leaders and civilizations being separated, and some civs have genuinely interesting identities that can change how you play.

The problem is that the Age system seems to constantly work against that organic feeling.

Within an Age, I can finally get my empire running the way I want it. My cities are developed, my economy starts connecting properly, my military has a purpose, and I begin building momentum. Then the Age ends.

Resources change or disappear, policies and slots are reset, City-State investments lose relevance, buildings become less valuable, tech and civic trees are replaced, and the next Age starts with another period of rebuilding and unlocking basic parts of its identity.

Exploration is probably the clearest example. You enter the "Exploration Age", but spend a significant part of it unlocking the ability to properly explore the open ocean. Modern feels similar: the more interesting modern military tools, especially aircraft and stronger units, arrive relatively late. By the time an Age really opens up, the next transition is already approaching.

Firaxis wanted to prevent snowballing and solve the supposedly boring late game. To me, they have mostly replaced one late game with several smaller periods where long-term investment starts feeling pointless because another reset is coming.

This also makes many strategic choices feel strangely artificial.

The Civic tree often feels like a collection of policies I will never slot and Wonders I may not even be able to place. Once I have the policies and traditions I actually want, large parts of the tree feel like prerequisites rather than meaningful development.

Victory conditions can be similarly unintuitive. A civilization focused almost entirely on Science is not necessarily progressing strongly toward a Science Victory unless it performs the specific actions that generate Innovation. Military victory heavily rewards simply owning settlements, meaning peaceful wide expansion can sometimes feel more rewarding than actually fighting effective wars.

That leads into another issue: wide play seems heavily favoured. A carefully developed compact empire can be satisfying to build, but raw settlement count gives access to so many more resources, buildings, trade opportunities and victory points that playing tall often feels like something you do because you enjoy it, not because the game rewards it equally.

And that is probably my biggest problem with Civ VII.

It often feels like the game wants me to play the systems rather than build a civilization.

Instead of asking "what would make my empire stronger?", I increasingly find myself asking "what does this leader, civ, Age or victory condition specifically want me to do right now?"

That does create interesting builds, and some combinations are genuinely fun. But it also makes the game feel more fragmented and gamey than I expected from Civilization.

What makes this frustrating is that underneath all of this I can see a version of Civ VII that I would probably love. The combat is good. Commanders are excellent. Towns supporting Cities is a great idea. Trade feels meaningful. Some civ designs are much more interesting than simple percentage bonuses.

But the Age structure keeps interrupting the parts I enjoy most.

Even after more than 60 hours, I am still trying to learn how Civilization VII wants to be played instead of feeling like I am naturally building my own civilization.

I don't think Civ VII is a bad game. I think it is an ambitious game with several genuinely good ideas tied together by a progression system that, for me, repeatedly kills its own momentum.

For now, I cannot fully recommend it — but I also haven't stopped playing it.

I have been a fan of this franchise since Civ 5, and I'd love to tell you why I love Civ 7.
First.. through a lens of its criticisms: COST and AGE REGROUP rework.

COST TLDR-- Love that Firaxis hasn't paywalled the playability of this game through its additional content/leader pack DLC's, and committed to free improvements/updates. Buy what you can, or wait for a sale--the gameplay remains the same for all!
COST::
I actually really like the way that Firaxis has chosen to release this game. Largely the comments about this game being overpriced come down to the content packs/DLC's that have been added. What is nice, is that I think the game is completely playable without any additional DLC's. The added content at release is overpriced, I agree, though they are completely unnecessary in enjoying the actual game. I felt like Civ 6 was largely not enjoyable until AFTER its first major expansion was released that added more gameplay functionality. It's reassuring that Firaxis has added multiple updates for free (one major game update already, and another now, at the time of this review 9/15/26). If you can afford the DLC's, feel free to support the game, otherwise wait for a big sale.. but I do like that the core game's additions aren't paywalled, which is what MOST other games do, and what most fans expect when purchasing additional content. 

AGE REGROUP TLDR-- FIRST this is already addressed in the first major game update: They reworked the game by breaking it down into three ages: Antiquity, Exploration, and Modern ages, which I REALLY like. It makes the game bite sized with each age feeling like its own playable short segment of the game. (I can do a 3-5 hour session with one age instead of having to marathon an entire playthrough with 14+ hours, OR come back to an increasingly hectic game days or a week later). It focuses civ abilities within each so all civs are relevant at every Age that you play in too!

AGE REGROUP::  
Apex Age: All civs are classified into Aniquity, Exploration, or the Modern Age making their abilities relevant at each stage of the game. You CAN play any civ in each, but Apex civs get their bonus units and abilities within their respective age. ((No more playing as America with a unique P-51 plane and film studio which you don't get to until the end of the game! In Civ 7, you can play them in the modern age after progressing through two other civs respective Apex ages. Remember you CAN change this option)). If your abilities work for the session you are in, you can keep your civ and unlock other abilities through the same civics tree through a new mechanic called 'Syncretism', OR pick a new Apex civ. This makes abilities (mentioned below) like religion or planes more relevant for the age they exist in.

Length of Ages-- I started SO MANY Civ 5 and 6 games that I only got halfway through because city management, and worker and unit actions just got SO HECTIC. I can't play for 14+ straight hours, so digesting each one in its own play session keeps me engaged through the end, every time for me. And the reset isn't so bad. It makes each era feel fresh and relevant with new strategies. ((Maybe I was losing Antiquity militarily and I can progress from Greece to the Normans, which are a scientific AND defensive civ having fortifications bonuses?? )). This does majorly disrupt the traditional way to play the game in previous CIV titles, but I think it improves where Civ 5 and 6 just.. dragged on.

HERE IS WHAT I REALLY LIKE::
Cities and Towns: 
I love how the settlement cap works within cities and towns. You only have to manage a handful of city's build actions in Civ 7. Everything else starts out as towns that can later be specialized to help cities grow via farming or mining towns, increase culture or science yields as urban centers, improve trade and happiness bonuses as trading outposts and resort towns, OR function as strategic/defensive military settlements as fort towns. Gone also are workers and endless (and quite frankly, kinda pointless) micromanagement. Every population bump in a city/settlement either adds another yield tile, or adds a specialist to an urban 'district'.  

Settlements RANT:: 
I HATED the Civ 6 expansion strategy of frantically just trying to wood chop out a settler to expand to the perfect spot, because early military was just SO costly to try to capture an opponents settlement if he got there first (and the advantage of early settlements meant you had 10-40 turns of population growth to a city). You can only get to half the map in the Antiquity in Civ 7 anyways, so it DOESN'T MATTER. Focus your cultural yields! Focus your science! If you're a military civ, it's not a huge impediment to your own growth to go take another settlement if your neighbor overextends and has a weak approach to military strategy. It felt like Civ 6 punished you for military expansion if someone else had the technological edge on you with a higher tier unit. Combat felt like it was far weaker than just simply having a better expansion strategy, SO YOU HAD TO DIVERSIFY WITH ALL THESE SPECIAL MILITARY COUNTER UNITS. Combat in Civ 7 is much simpler, and it is self contained within each age. I've spent the Antiquity pummeling my neighbor, just to ally and trade with him in Exploration Age as we both go off in opposing directions to settle distant lands.

Military::
Oh wow! It's refreshing that this isn't overly complicated, yet still tactically engaging and WAY MORE FUN. They reworked Great Generals into Army or Fleet or Squadron Commanders. Now you have simpler unit types that are either enhanced by Army Commander Abilities or civics abilities (which makes civics so relevant from a defensive perspective). Yes, the unit types are simpler, but it's not impossible to hold off an attack with an earlier tier unit, OR conquer and hold a settlement if you're technologically behind. Army commanders make combat WAY more strategic by allowing you to withdraw/deploy units more flexibly, exercise special combat tactics, or maneuver terrain to overcome positioning. It focuses the combat from just reaching higher tier units to a dynamic tactical strategy by multiple types of commanders.

Religion: 
Because the game is split into multiple ages, it makes everything more relevant. Religion in Antiquity is a basic bonus applied to settlements with altars.. In Exploration you have missionaries that can convert other cities for your specific purpose (you select one specific way to acquire relics for culture, and then a yield type that focuses science, culture, or maybe a military enhancement). It's no longer a win condition and sits on the side as an enhancement you CAN pursue, or something that you lean on to give you a big leap. You can't get locked out of a religion like you did in Civ 6, and you don't reach end game basically "fighting" another version of combat for a religious victory via "religious combat".

Triumphs, Dedications, and Victory Conditions::
Seldom mentioned, but this is what the game is really about! You get a list of triumphs to achieve within each Age that unlock dedications you can select in the next. Some give immediate bonuses, and others allow you to plan some of the next age's strategies. I like that Civ 7 also unlocks WHICH civs you progress to in the next era conditionally. If you settle next to a bunch of mountains, you unlock the Incas, which can work mountain tiles in Exploration (before Modern). Dedications are bonuses that make each game feel more focused for YOUR strategy.

There is so much more, but I think this game does so much right! It mitigates hard RNG factors in Civ 5 and 6 and makes the game more flexible and exciting to play. I play above middle difficulty, and would say it's got an easier learning curve for new players and deeper strategies for veterans. All around, I think it's the best installment in the series and it is only getting better.

Played for a short time over a free weekend, and the fact I feel enough gameplay was experienced to leave a review after only period should speak volumes enough. It feels somewhere between your half-baked, diamond in the rough we've come to expect in this section of the gaming market, and a well polished turd, that is still a turd no matter how much shiny bits you add to it. 

The key takeaway is that Civ7 feels like a total (unnecessary) simplification of the Civilization series while delivering some of the requested features that would have made Civ5 and Civ6 even better sequels. Trading navigable rivers and the village/town/city system for a completely gutted out research tree and the Ages system is something I wouldn't have done (and the lack of shift+click queuing in base game for some reason)  -- innovating for the sake of saying you did rather than looking at popular modded in features from previous games or redesigning less than welcomed features to be more in line with what made other entries, successful.

Perhaps in time, with enough free updates, Civ7 can be on the same basis as say Civ5, but then the devs will have to contend with having a game, several years post-release, be on the same level as a previous Civ game was on Day 1, but until then, I'm firmly meh about the game.

Civ 7 isn't as good as civ 6.  Civ 7 is more frustration than fun.

Positives:
City growth, population management and worker management have all changed for the better.  Natural wonders aren't too overpowered and the management around bonus/special resources works better than in other civ games.  In general, some of the gameplay feels fairly well polished and there are some new mechanics around ages and crisis that can help levelset against runaway dominations adding some later game challenge.  I appreciate the new mechanics, though I could have gone a different way, but in all not a negative.  Stacking lots of small bonuses works better than a bunch of large bonuses.  Diplomacy is a bit easier and used more often.

The bad:
Well, almost everything else.  This is a regression backwards to where you have to click on every single thing every single round.  It quickly starts to feel more like work and micromanagement than playing a game.
Can't autoexplore with anything but a scout, autoexplore consistently breaks - even though old autoexplore would go and get loot huts for you.
Ships around a coast require attention every round
Every single city expansion has to be individually managed, land acquisition cannot be automated or queued, all individual cities can't autodecide either because of the way districts are setup.
Every age change is a regression in which cities and resources reset, breaking a lot of progress and setting you back at every age.
Can't queue research well, All I can do is click to a later research which will skip the "2s" of many side researches.
Army integration is really bad, unpacking needs to happen on a per unit basis in many cases because the unpacking will often put units in bad locations, IE archers on the front line instead of in the rear.  Generals, even though they have a stack on them are the ones that take damage first when attacked by other units, breaking the army.
Ship pathing always selects to go into deep water when they will take damage - for naval, settlers and everything.  It doesn't even bother with fastest path, which could take a settler 2 further land hexes to have a faster water crossing, it only takes the shortest drawn path.
Pathing for units is really bad, I can't tell if a unit will do what I want it to do before it moves, if I tell it to attack an adjacent tile, it might do it, or it might not.  If there's a cliff that I can't see, it will path many hexes around instead of confirming that's what I want to do.  If it's on a hex with a general it may do this anyway even though there's a clear path to attack.  There's a consistency for units to be in boat formation when on rivers, even after making it to an age where roads are common, which requires for the enemy to make bridge districts to make my armies work - which never happens.  Also bridge districts are a waste.
Descriptions don't align correctly with some actions, like the razing of a city either doesn't work correctly with the influence description or has an incorrect description.  Same with descriptions on some of the cards around specialist upkeep.
The map generator isn't great, biomes don't feel cohesive or interesting.
Setting up armies is neither great nor convenient and many of the promotion abilities are not good, but are required to get to necessary ones.
Starting a new game doesn't preserve the settings that I have to recreate every time, saving settings forces a save of the map seed.
Autocycle units only half works, sometimes it will go on to the next unit, like for attacking and moving, but not for other commands like upgrades and sometimes on movement if I queue outside of the range.
Upgrading units when in an army is way too many clicks, and a bad interface.
Nothing is explained in the game, if a unit doesn't have line of sight to hit something, there's no description telling you what's wrong, if something doesn't work or is unavailable, it just doesn't work, always making me wonder if it didn't take my input or if there's a real reason it doesn't work.
Setting up trade routes is pretty dumb, I have to send the trader out to a city and then establish a trade route, instead of setting it all up in one click.  This also means you have to manually track all trade routes.
Setting up as suzerian for city states is way worse than civ 6 and resets every age.

As a long time Civ franchise player I had held off playing Civ 7 mainly due to the radical changes made with the forced age system, lack of civilization continuality (at the time of launch), plus other questionable game design choices. With the free week of play I decided to give Civ 7 a try to see if lived up to my fears and the hate the game has received.

In short, the hate and my fears of the game were indeed warranted. Civ 7 does not feel like a civ game, it feels like something else, like a cousin but not direct family to the series. The game continously wants you to play a certain way, it feels confined and convoulted when playing. It does not feel like the traditional sandbox of previous civ games. Rather than me commanding my civ through the ages with Civ 7 I feel like am just along from the ride, a bus ride, not a comfortable one.

For me I just can't really get over this new age system, it's terrible and horribly implemented. While it may have sounded good on paper in practice it was a real bad idea. They were trying to solve a problem that didn't need to be solved (snowballing). What they should have done instead of civ switching each age they should have had different leader options for your chosen civ, that would have made more sense.

The good in Civ 7 is the beautiful graphics, this is what I had wanted with Civ 6 instead of the cartoony graphics, Civ 7 is definately a beautiful game. That said I had heard some people complain it's hard to understand the city sprawl/district tiles and I get that but that doesn't bother me much. Navigateable rivers is also a great addition.

Other things that were not great but I could overlook, the UI of the game feels very clunky and bloated, feels like it was definately not designed with a PC focus otherwise you wouldn't make everything so bulky wasteful of space. I also do not like the Leader graphics/animations or the diplomacy interaction screens, go back and compare it to Civ 5 for example and you can see how much of a downgrade it is, the 3rd person view also hurts immersion.

I am not sure if Civ 7 can be properly salvaged, it's now more than a year plus since release and the fixes they have done still feel lacking, the game still feels very incomplete. I played a complete game and it was dissappointing, the victory felt empty like I didn't really deserve it, I barely did anything and got a military victory.

What I would really like is true classic mode of play. No forced age resets, just continious play throughout the ages, however given the game design choices I doubt this will ever happen and that unfortunately is kind of a deal breaker for me. This incomplete game also needs the modern era and a proper earth map (which at lease appears to be coming in the near future).

If there is another free weekend or if the completed game is super cheap in a few years I will give it another try but for now I can't recommend it and not eager to play it at all, I will just go back to playing Civ 4-6. I hope they make better game design choices (Firaxis needs a new design lead as Ed Beach appears not up to the task) for Civ 8 and I hope they move on from Civ 7 sooner rather than later as I think it's just throwing good money after bad at this point.

Feedback to the devs.  

Plain bugs:
1. Commander abilities.
-- Sometimes adjacent units won't fire upon the target of Focus Fire despite, immediately after using the ability, I can order that unit to fire upon the exact same target without any issue. 
-- Similarly, sometimes melee units ignore the Coordinated Attack ability. 
2. The blue polygon which indicates unit movement limit sometimes exclude reachable tiles. When I hold my right mouse button over such a tile it shows "1" and when I release RMB my unit travel to the tile absolutely fine. 
3. For once the "Pick Dedications for New Age" option did not appear. In fact I forgot they ever existing until 3 turns into the Exploration Age. 
4. The same notifications of another civilization becoming the Suzerain of a city states and receiving gifts appear every few turns despite I having marked them as read with right clicks. 
5. The camera often flies off to nowhere when tutorial windows pop up.

Possible bugs:
1. Recommended settlement locations (the tall building icon) are inconsistent despite no observable change in the vicinity. It may disappear on the next turn and then reappear another one after. For once when I finally have my Settler reach a recommended location, the icon moves to an adjacent tile. 
2. Sometimes unit-built fortifications are not drawn: The build option is disabled ("fortification already exists at this location") although the usual clay and stakes are not present around the tile. 
3. More of Commander abilities. 
-- Occasionally melee units out of attack range respond to Coordinated Attack my moving towards the target. 
-- I almost always have the first Logistic promotion. It is somewhat unpredictable whether a unit leaving the commander can act after doing so. 

UI improvements:
1. Tooltips often leave out important information.
-- Tech tree tooltips should show build cost and maintenance cost of buildings, units, and wonders - If you show bonuses then why not show negative bonuses? At least take me to the the encyclopedia page. 
-- The trade route panel opened with the selection of a Merchant should show the bonus of each resources on top of how much gold my trade partner may gain. Arguably I care more about the former than the latter. 
-- The Trade Route tab that shows existing Trade Routes and possible Trade Routes at the moment should also show possible Trade Routes after an Improve Trade Relation Endeavor. Otherwise it is difficult to tell if I should improve trade relations. 
2. The UI should indicate how many moves a unit will have left when the player hovers over a tile. 
3. It should be easier for new players to tell whether an item on the tech tree and the civic tree is a policy, a tradition, or a passive bonus. 
4. Tiles design. I mistook a desert / steppe tile as Vegetated. Sometimes the lighting makes me wonder if a tile is covered by fog of war or revealed. 

Gamplay and experience:
I used to play FreeCiv (Civ 2) and Unciv (Civ 5). This is the first official game I play (so I am from not your core player base). Since I never loved how the series theorize about historical development - it is a valid way, but not one I deem worth iterating over and over - I welcome the experimentations in Civ 7. 
(No, I am neither a historian nor anthropologist)
I don't agree at all having to 'switch civilization' breaks the historical realism or gameplay immersion of building a civilization. If I may be so bold to say that the nationalist education we receive these days about cultural or ethnic heritage and unity are often rather far-fetched. Let's take the USSR as an example. It was quite the polar opposite in terms of ideology, society, and economy from the Tsarist Russia, but one has to admit that they are arguably the same civilizaton (an ambiguous term, maybe in Huntington's sense here) - the people lives on from one to the other, the leaders lived in and then reacted to the challenges in the former age, both are constrained and motivated by the same natural and artificial environment. The point is that what we can call a civilization is usually not a homogenous entity, but rather a hotchpotch of the consequences of historical development. I think city structures (buildings, Wonders, urbanization), Traditions, and leader Attribute Points have the potential to represent that. (Of course the USSR is not only Russia, but does that not make my point of 'civilizations' being heterogenous in time and space stronger?)
I can also accept the existence of Age Transition. I think it is mostly for giving the weaker civs a chance of making a comeback - breaking sieges, preventing technological snowballing, controlling new-age resources. It faintly reminds me of Late Bronze Age collapse. As many board games have such stage / phase mechanics and it being somewhat historical, I am fine with that. That being said, I suggest optional softening of Age Transition, such as an age transition period of like 8 turns, during which
-- diplomacy
---- relation decays quicker and depending on the relation (relative to customizable values) war and alliance may end
-- technology
---- civs may begin to research next-age techs with some customizable restrictions or penalties

The problems I have with the game are:
1) Lots of bugs as listed above. Many more encountered by other players. 
2) Poor UI designs as listed above. 
3) Lacking explanations. For example, 
-- I can't tell precisely when I receive a tradition slot despite having played for so long. 
-- The "does not end movement on (e.g. vegetated) tile" perks seems to prevent ending movement because of, for example, minor river on a vegetated tile. However, sometimes it does not prevent that. I don't know how it works. 
-- I believe a unit fortifying a district does not make the tile a "Fortified District" (?)
-- I spent a lot of time figuring out that I cannot 'upgrade' improvements on a resource tile to a Hillfort. 
-- I cannot pack my Army Commander under a Fleet Commander. 
4) Long loading time. 
5) The game is expensive. 

The free week was nice, but I don't think the game is ready yet.

1. My personal favorite changes mostly come in the form of combat/military mechanics, the commanders feel fresh and nice to use and the pace of war feels close to perfect, even on shorter time modes where military struggled in 6. The best changes though are the fact the AI actually fight back in this game, it's not perfect (they're still pretty dumb and don't use boats or commanders well) but they have actual militaries that put pressure on you, unlike civ 6 where they might give a passable resistence at the start of the war but quickly just lie down and die, and then there's seperating units and resources, a sour spot I had in 6 was you could be hindered in some aspects based purely on resource spawns (the most obvious being uranium and oil), civ 7 ditches resources being a requirement and instead change them to be combat strength buffs for specific types of units, giving you and advantage for still having them but not completely locking you out of the mechanic

2. The gameplay is more varied in ways to play: while on release it was a rightfully mocked concept seperating the leaders and civilizations allows for more varied gameplay styles, and example i've liked is the civ of Carthage in the antiquity age's main mechanic is only having one city, but gaining two settlers (more specifically their unique settlers) and merchants whenever they produce or purchase them. This would kill a leader in civ 6 with how restrictive it is but here it's a tool to let you scale up your civilization faster, as you can use it to quickly build your empire and establish trade routes but then switch to a different civ when the age transitions where you are more punished for not having multiple cities. The leader's themselves also feel varied and rarely overlap, you have best boy Gilgamesh who finds his one true ally and fights to the end for them, Ibn Battuta who's all about vision and map knowledge and being able to pivot his playstyle based on the circumstances, Harriet Tubman who focuses of espionage while having a defense against retaliation if found out by making wars against her give serious war weariness, and that's just a small pool, there's even what i'd call a "tutorial" leader with Confucious who has the most basic passives that still let you experiment but more importantly just figure out the games mechanics without having to worry about optimizing your leader's potential.

3. The artstyle: the visuals on the game are very well made and is a great blend between civ 5's realism and 6's more cartoon style, unit models feel fantastic and the animations help war feel like war instead of a chess game, the music is still quality work and the narrator does her job well.

4. Science: military and science are by far the most "simple" ways to go through the game but with the changes to victory conditions science gets more depth as you still have the same goal plan of dominating the tech tree and completing projects the fastest they also have to play a balancing act for the other game types, if they just ignore economy, culture, or military they risk the enemy getting too far ahead and reaching a victory threshold before they can reach the modern age and space race technologies, so they always have to try and be competitive  with a military force and control while sticking in striking distance of tourism or GDP if things start to look dire in those areas

NUETRALS:
Now we reach the things I'm not so certain about or feel like I don't have enough experience with to give as concrete of an answer for:

1. Religion and Culture: religion wasn't really something i used much in civ 6, but was still a fine addition with it's own style, even if it wasn't to everyones taste with the seperate religious wars and the mechanics surronding it, but religion in civilization is just cultural, there some other benefits for it but it's main purpose is for getting relics in the exploration age, which are a core part of culture's victory path, tying these two together which just doesn't feel right to me, there's also the fact that there isn't really anything you can do to stop it, you can't kill missionaries so they're just allowed to walk into your empire and start converting things with the only way to fight it is just spawning more missionaries of your own the reconvert them, the system is also cheesable for the same reason, you can get your relics for converting but then just ignore it for the rest of the age, but put a few missionaries on other players settlements and then on the last few turns have them mass convert them to go into modern with a MASSIVE advantage, and again there's no stopping it as missionaries are unkillable.
As for culture outside the exploration age and it's ties to religion it also suffers issues from what feel like an unfinished system, it has the same plan as 6: Collect great works, wonders, and have good appeal across your empire to raise tourism... the problem is there's no great people in this game so your great relics are Codices in antiquity (resource for science), relics in exploration (tied to religion as discussed), and artefacts (excavations in the modern age, needing to send a slow unit across the map to maybe find something), without music, art, or sculptures that civ 6 had it makes it feel flat and seriously bogged down when the other playstyles were elevated, hopefully they will add more depth to the system later down the line when more crucial changes are amde (we'll get to those)

2.AI difficulty scaling: Civilization has always struggled with AI difficulty and i fully know this will never be "solved". Civ 7 makes some changes from 6 in terms of increasing difficulty, in 6 it would just give the AI plenty of free tools: more settlers, bonus units, etc. in 7 they did away with that style (which i like, the ai having multiple cities before you even had the chance to get a 2nd wasn't very interesting IMO) but replaced it with just MASSIVE modifiers for everything, this makes the early game feel AWFUL, you'll never get wonders unless they have very specific requirements or the ai are just programmed to not bother with them until later on. Have a wonder that's crucial to a playstyle like Collosal for resource capacity in economic? too bad even if you rush the rech and start the production as soon as possible you still won't finish it before the ai, and good luck getting Hanging Gardens. but the thing is once you reach the exploration phase you can quickly pass the ai and snowball to victory, the makes the early game incredibly frustrating but the end game not really feel any different. My solution would just be an option to have the modifiers progress as the ages do (which is a mod) so you can feel at least somewhat equal in antiquity but the modifiers would let them become more competitive threats in exploration and modern.

I played during the free weekend with a friend and here are my take aways: (conclusion: worth $30 definably not 70)

The Bad:
1. the Ai doesn't build walls so a single general can wipe a civ out
2. city states are "first come first serve" where boosting relations are worthless unless 2 people found the city sate within 5 turns and if you loose/know you will loose you can kill it before it becomes a city state
3. Age transitions screw all trade and resources, force you to spend 1 of 3 dedications on keeping your cities, destroys your social/traditions slots, removes and spawns new city states and generally leave you rebuilding for ~20% of the current age
4. we got put into a loading screen about twice per age along with the age transition loading. (the loading wasn't that slow, but was annoying)
5. certain civics/techs provide espionage/agreement actions for you to make with other leader, but are forever unavailable if you don't research them before the age ends.
6. Gold (apart from the "giving aid" endeavor), influence, and cities can only be traded in a peace agreement and are impossible to trade without going to war first

The Neutral:
1. Generals can be reinforced (I love this) and tend to act as an infinite spawner (My friend hated this)
2. My empire yields felt pretty random as they would increase and decrease despite minimal influence on that stat (maybe I'm bad at the game, but 30 science per turn lost from thin air from seemingly nothing hurts)
3. most city state buffs/social policies focused on city states are heavily reliant on have other city sates sometimes of a specific type and city states themselves are too common
4. Age transitions end wars and converts existing units to their upgraded form so no unit from a previous age exists in the current era (even if it is a unique unit farther on the tech tree)

The Good:
1. There is some meta progression
2. civ changing is fun
3. armies are easier to move as groups using generals (technically army commanders or navy commanders)
4. city states provide several buffs to choose from which can be pretty valuable
5. The exploration age strongly encourages overseas colonies, which gives the same vibes as the historical time period
6. just about all diplomacy requires influence to give a positive or negative response including maximizing benefits form a joint endeavor form another civ
7. the resource trade mechanic using traders is much better than civ 6's trade mechanic (using traders)

Played this game during free week and wanted to give it a fair review. There are many negative reviews and many feel unfair. If you put 800+ hours into a game, then you got your money's worth. You didn't hate it so much to go play Civ V or Civ VI instead or to return the game. Why hate something so much and spend so much time on it? Meanwhile, there are reviews saying it's awful with only 15 minutes recorded time... That gets you through initial setup, hardly a fair shot at the game and not enough time to experience the main mechanic people complain about. Honestly set up is very similar to previous games in the series. 

As of this review, I have played 48 hours, My wife and I played 1 standard length game over LAN, and I made it through about half of a quick game before time ran out. We both have many hours of experience in previous Civ games. 

[h3]Things we liked: [/h3]
[list]
[*]Characters presented and the ability to mix and match with Civilizations, many characters are new and not from the general mix that the previous games rotate through.
[*]Economic victory being a win condition.
[*] Streamlining on citizen management.
[*]Commanders can carry units.
[*]Narration events
[*] Influence/diplomacy system
[*] Early espionage
[*]The city states/barbarians. Pretty similar to 6, you pay them and they eventually become not hostile. They weren't so bad to limit what cities were developing significantly.
[*]Town to city progression, towns made it easier to spread wide.
[*]Ran fine on my laptop on default settings, though I have a gaming laptop with good specs.
[*] No workers, I honestly forgot that they didn't exist, that's how little I missed them.
[*]Unique animation at the end for the victor's character was a nice touch.
[/list]

[h3]Mixed:[/h3]
[list]
[*]We had different opinions on commanders vs units gaining experience.
[*]Meta progression is kind of weird for a civ game, we don't fully hate it, just find it odd.
[/list]


[h3]Things we think could be better: [/h3]
[list]
[*]Religion. Overpowered in 6, but only mildly important in 1 age of the game in 7.
[*]User interface.
[list]
[*]How do we cycle through units? No idea. 
[*]Where is my boat set to auto explore? Gotta look over the map until I find it. 
[*]Merchants will ask where to start trade then ask again when they arrive... I thought they had completed routes and were wanting to start another route (oops my poor guys just running everywhere). 
[*]"Other Yields" really should be broken down or a hover list to show where the resources are coming from. My wife asked me how I was making so much money, and we had no idea, because I couldn't remember what things I had done to get +$### in my "other yields" box.
[/list]
[/list]

[list]
[*]No statistics at the end of the game, you can see all the charts you can see during the game. But you can't see things like "how much money each civ had over time" or how many units someone had. Previous games had a lot of charts that are missing here.
[*]There doesn't seem to be a way to know military strength between yourself and other nations and military score isn't reliable for this if no one is conquering. 
[*]I have this complaint about all civ games in general, the inability to rotate the map. I want to see my Colossus wonder from the front view, yet because of the tile I used, I only get his backside (Wonder finished animations exist in single player only). It would be nice to not be stuck to north always at top of screen. It doesn't even need to be a globe, just allow the flat plane to rotate, maybe have a true north compass at the top that can keep it locked at north/reset back to north. I'm sure the fixed camera angled fixes a lot of graphic optimizations, but it feels like it should be doable.
[*]We don't like the DLC model, many of the DLCs look like they should be in the base game... I don't feel like I should have to pay $7.25NZD to have the second half of a character that already exists in the game.
[*]Paying for towns to become cities again in the next age.
[*]Putting "police state" under communism is a choice that was made. The government "ideologies" could be better as the 3 presented could all technically exist in a single government system. 
[/list]


[h3]Bugs: [/h3]
We didn't encounter many, but we had issues with roads. I had a road between 2 cities in age 1 that broke in age 2 and the only fix seemed to be to put a city in between the 2 settlements. Trying to use a merchant to fix the road didn't seem to work. There was visibly a road in each tile. We had some crashing issues, but we aren't sure if that is a game issue or a router issue on our end.

[h3]Final thoughts:[/h3]
Overall, we enjoyed the game. We're still debating on purchasing since we own 5 and 6, though leaning toward buying. My wife did say if we went back to 6, she would miss some of the things in 7.

The age system was jarring the first time we experienced it, but after that age transitions were no big deal. I think it's only jarring because you don't know what to anticipate with the next age. 

Despite the rubber banding mechanics, my wife still managed to snow ball with 1000+ culture per turn while myself being closer to the AI's with only 200 culture per turn... in age 2... by age 3 her science was also that high.

Graphically, it's very pretty. I didn't think it looked crazy different than Civ 6. Animations seem higher quality. The unexplored tiles look nice.

It was pretty easy to pick up with previous Civilization series knowledge. There were a few instances of needing to look up how something worked, but that exists in other Civ games as well - that's why civilopedia exists in every single title... and sometimes you just need to play and see what happens on your first play through. 

Overall it still looked and felt like a Civ game.

I was playing Civ when many here were still in diapers. It was one of my very first PC games and if you would ask where I have spent most of my gaming hours over the years, Civ sits in the top 3.

I absolutely abhorred the idea that Civ 7 made us change our civilization. The idea was 'stolen' from Humankind, but it wasn't that great there either. It put me off. So did the reports of its shoddy UI and many other issues. 7 was the first Civ I did not play within a week of release. 

It took Firaxis ages (pun) to fix losing your civilization. Shame on them, truly. And for releasing it in such a bad state too. What a breach of trust.

A free week of Civ allowed me to check it out without Steam's prohibitive 2 hour return window. And you know what, Civ 7 is fine. I do have some issues with it, but it is sufficiently worthy and it does have some nice ideas (I particularly enjoy over building, army leaders and diplomacy).

It is not Civ 3 (my pinacle) or Civ 4 (a close second), but it is a Civ game, and deserving of the name.

@Firaxis - Should you read it, trust comes on foot and leaves by horse. You have not earned it back yet. If your current developers and designers do not understand the series they are meant to be championing, you should look for new ones. We all want you to experiment, refine, renew, but the very basic premise of Civ is to take your civilization and lead it through the ages. Break that, and you have something else.

Graphic is top-notch, no contest here. But still too many wall of texts and unclear instructions to new players. Some interesting gameplay mechanics and especially the leaders are well designed, very enjoyable. Prepare for huge learning curve. Buy when ON SALE only.

Honestly, I've played pretty much every Civ entry since Civilization III, and this one takes the cake in my book. I've really enjoyed getting my feet wet in this particular game and am looking forward to many more hours of "just one more turn." I know Civ VII has gotten a lot of flak and some of it is understandable, but the game is changing for the better, and there are hopefully greater things on the horizon. 

All in all, I love the graphics, the city sprawl, the story/narrative aspects, the unit design, the nation/leader combos, and I don't mind the nation switching so much. I am however, still trying to get used to the crisis and age change, I like some aspects and am turned off by others; but not so much that I won't keep coming back for more. 

I usually wait for sales here on Steam, so if you want the best bang for your buck, I highly recommend holding off until the price drops again before picking it up. If you can go in with an open mind and grab it on a discount, it's a worthy addition to the franchise.

It is what it says on the box: three (soon to be four) ages, some things endure and some don't, switching to new civ when entering new age (with recommendations that are at least plausible for your leader), etc. I feel that a lot of people who are still complaining just either didn't look at what they were getting in to, or just want to play the same Civ they've always played.

Not as bad I had heard (though the Test of Time update may have helped), but still not a game I'd buy over playing VI instead.

There are some improvements over the previous installment.  Diplomacy works better without requiring an alliance for everything.  Religion isn't as grindy and obnoxious.  The triumph system is a neat take on the gold/dark age system, giving various side objectives to focus on.

However, I really disliked the era system and the reset of the map. At the end of an era, all your cities downgrade back into towns (the whole town/city mechanic is also clunky and not great) unless you burn a dedication on preserving them.  The resources on the map completely change, so there's no planning ahead from previous eras.  You're also restricted to that era's techs and civics, and it seems to provide a soft-reset of AI power level.  All of this combines to lower the value of your strategic choices, particularly during the final turns of an era where what you produce can be literally thrown away by the era transition. I much prefer how in previous installments you'd lay the groundwork for your empire and then build up to a grand payoff, whereas here it felt like right as everything was finally falling into place, the end of an era counter would kick in and undo all that work.

There's also a lot of questionable decisions with the UI and UX of the game.  For some actions you need to right-click, but in other places right-click cancels the action.  However, on some screens like the Resource Assignment window, right-click doesn't cancel your resource assignment; it closes the window.

I also found it odd that all the city details are obscured by default, such as food surplus, happiness (despite happiness tier mattering for celebration policies), and specialists.  I could not for the life of me figure out what my specialists were producing in a given city and what their upkeep was, outside of the pop assignment window, and that's a problem because specialist output changes frequently throughout the eras and via your policy selections.  It's also annoying that many of the policies that impact your empire don't show you the impact, e.g. a policy that might add 1 science output to specialists should tell you what the total gain from that policy will be, considering once you slot it you're locked into your policies until the next civic is researched.  Likewise with the town specializations, where you have to pick a unique mutually-exclusive specialization for your town among various bonuses, but have to manually mouse over each hex on the map to figure out e.g. how many quarters that town has to see what the benefit of a particular specialization is (not to mention, it was totally unclear what town production was even for, given towns don't have a production queue).  Additionally, the map is hard to tell what was going on visually - with it not being clear why sometimes enemies two hexes away were in range of a shot or not.  Or even what types of terrain were on a hex.  I unlocked Russia by setting three tundra cities all the while thinking they were regular grassland tiles because anything that's not a desert looks similar to one another.  Not to mention, it's difficult to tell at a glance the difference between a Quarter and a District.

All in all, I'd give the game about a 4/10.  I'm sure it's improved since release, but I don't really feel the desire to play this over something like Civ VI or another 4X.  And that's without considering all the additional purchases accompanying the game.

I think they fixed some of the initial complaint stuff people had. Overall I am liking VII more than I liked VI, but it's nowhere near the game V or IV was. 

Stuff I enjoyed:

Commanders make the terrain feel more impactful in combat. Being able to stack your units on one unit, to get around a chokepoint from terrain felt incredibly refreshing. No more having to move units one by one through a 2 hex wide area, only for the enemy to have spawned 3-4 new fresh units to finish off your frontline veteran units before you could pull them back to re-supply. 

The progression from founding small towns to boost your capital city production, with the ability to turn them into cities later for gold was also interesting. It felt like a more natural way of expansion than I'd experienced before.

Some things I didn't enjoy:

Settlement cap was incredibly annoying, and is like a direct middle-finger to the fast expansion playstyle. feels like some totally unnecessary artificial difficulty modifier just to say they wanted to make the game more challenging. 

I still find districts an annoying departure from how CIv cities should work, it was my biggest complaint from VI, but I will admit at least it is a little improved in VII.

The age system is incredibly jarring, to switch up the core fundamentals of your empire seems entirely counterinuitive to how the game used to play. I get it is a new game and they were trying new things, but I would prefer that the way a civilization progresses to a new age simply upgrades the look of the map and the tech tree, maybe a bonus or demerit based on how well you've been playing. That's it. 


Overall it gets a solid 7/10 for me, and I will probably pick it up during a future sale when there's been a little more DLC released.

7: districts better. Build quarters & can “build over” them. Although no choice of which one to overbuild, & even if there's a free slot, current age district will overbuild old district anyway. Pretty dumb.
7: resources, kinda better &worse at the same time.
Strategic resources; gone. Kinda. No need to find iron, oil, or niter. Get bonus to producing its associated units if you have it. Luxuries too.
Each settlement has its own happiness like in earlier civ games, but I didn't really notice it affecting anything except Antiquity end crisis. & since the game uses ages instead of eras, & they're exactly the same for everyone, we're back to civ 5 “golden age”s, (celebrations), & you can choose one of two bonuses determined by your government. Seems to usually be a trade-off of picking either a lump sum or bonus over time & 0 guarantee that bonus will ever actually get used.
No trade. Ever. Only time a tradescreen pops up: peace deals. & from what I saw (only played 1 long ages marathon game), can't trade cities captured from other civs. Ally forced me into a war with neighbour. Propose peace time, I had captured many cities from other civs because of my allies. So I wanted to give that civ a bunch of the captured cities so I could go under my settlement cap (or at least go down to only 5 over) & give them a boost. None of the cities I took except theirs & ones I settled myself, were options to give.
So. No trade. & unless I want to return the cities to the civs that attacked me, I had to deal with an influence penalty & over settlement penalties. Which made unhappiness. Cascades into a perpetual self-destruction loop.
Because I chose not to Raze the settlements & incur a much larger influence penalty for the remainder of the age.
Acquire resources from civs? Aside from simply taking the settlements that have them, your only other option is to build trading caravans. Which, along with every civilian unit, increases in cost after each acquisition of one. It's neat that you can use your influence to get a civ to agree to have more trade routes with you, instead of being locked into them by researching civics & having specific policies. I'll give it that. But it's really more like you're sending in goblins to clone the resources. It doesn't matter if a settlement only has 1 resource, you send a caravan in & both of you earn gold from'em & can slot'em in your settlements. So. No trading.
Resource slot screen has its own loading screen.
UI is bad. & manipulating the thing is a pain in the ass too. You'd think you can just click & drag & bam you're done, but no.
If the settlement you're dropping a resource into has 0 open slots, you cannot just drop it & swap the resource. You must remove the resource first. But you can't just double-click it to send it to the magic pocket dimension warehouse. You have to click, hold, drag. & you have to end that drag in the bar for unslotted resources. That seems like a no brainer, but it's 2026 & if I'm moving an item & it isn't being put into a specific slot I really do expect it to return to the pocket dimension from wherever I let go of it.
& it's so. Slow.
If I have 17 resource slots in a city, it can take over 3 minutes just from the time to click & drag items into empty slots. It's actually faster to press the “empty all” button on settlement side & reslot everything from scratch if going to make 4+ changes.
1-click select city, double-click item anywhere & it's added to the selected city, or it's removed if it was already in the city. Click off the city banner to deselect it. It isn't difficult. Not sure why a professional team of game devs couldn't make it. I'd say they built the game for smartphones with how simplified everything is, except the UI is so bad it wouldn't function. You wouldn't be able to war at all.
You have detailed lists of which cities have which resources you can exploit including where they're from, but there's no list anywhere of your units. If you sleep a unit, you'd better remember where you left them. Because there's no indication they even exist except looking directly at them. No list to see how many units you have or cycle through besides the game auto-centering on them when it thinks its the unit’s turn. You will lose track of civilians (like explorers). Units do not wake up when damaged by disasters.
You cannot search for resources or digsites either.
& don't even get me started on the “diplomacy” ribbon. Huge waste of space & the only way to shrink it is to shrink the entire UI.
Great people: Which only some civs get. In some ages. & only if you build that civs unique Quarter. & if you don't have that quarter in a city, you can only get the person with $.
The only way to get buildings in towns is $. All production is sent along your trade network to your cities. Give them a focus & they don't grow either.
1 non-growth focus per age. So you'd better know which 1 will suit them best. Not a big deal until the Modern (&final) Age, where factory focus isn't unlocked until later & only available if the town has a factory resource in its borders. & the factory focus is OP as ♥♥♥♥ because of how expensive rail stations, factories & ports are. Factory focus cuts their $ cost in half. It's better to keep your towns as towns until you buy factories in them & then turn them into cities, because the production to build them just isn't worth it.
In fact, you'll be buying most of your buildings. & units.
Production used to be able to churn out buildings, districts, & conga lines of units. Now?
Maybe it was how I played, but I never got above 80 production in a city. Modern Age: 50 turns to build the Eiffel tower, 34 turns for a laboratory.
& since I was too busy trying to get Wonders, all my $ went to buildings. Usually to get more $, so I could buy more buildings.
There is no substitute for $ in civ 7. I cannot be a production powerhouse. I must produce more $ than anything else.
& the AI didn't seem to get the memo.
Bots are very bad at the game. Caesar had over 10,000 $ at the end of a war with him once. Why hadn't he spent it? Military? Buildings? Settlers? Anything?
& until Modern Age, nobody but me ever seemed to have any military. Antiquity age, bots that attacked basically had 1 wave of military units, if that, & were easily stomped out. Exploration Age, no civ but me built privateers. No bots plundered trade routes or captured treasure convoys. Didn't even protect them.
But then in the modern age, everyone suddenly had anthills of landships to try & roll me over. Machiavelli even had a couple dreadnaughts on the seas.
Meanwhile I had armadas' of ships t1 to t3, because all my privateers were converted at the start of the new age.
I swear, if I had played as a maritime civ I would've won domination in the exploration age.
Because I won the military victory in the modern age before it had 25% progress. By accident.
Because my allies pulled me into wars, & I wanted to stop the congaline of landships (tier 2, btw) from attacking my settlements. & as I'm carpet-bombing Berlin & Paris in 1808, & plowing through landships with my modern tanks, I get a notification: Gilgamesh will win military victory in 5 turns.
& then I did. The war of 1812 was a world war, & I won.
I was going for economic & science victory. & accidentally dominated.
& I gotta clarify, I played one difficulty higher than “normal”. & I was making more money, science, & influence than every other civ combined, & then doubled. I was a bit behind in culture most of the time, but was still somehow ahead of Caesar, who was getting 900 culture per turn.
Most civs couldn't get more than 12 influence a turn. Half were getting negative influence each turn. I was getting over 200. I was researching nuclear fission in 1810.
I have more to say, specifically about the core mechanic of ages & how they're neat but poorly implemented & comparing to Humankind, but I'm tired & bored now. Gonna take a nap.

Unbalanced, Buggy, Unoptimized

(Played during a Free Weekend, 1 standard game ~ 12h)
This game reminded me how much I love Civ VI. Not because Civilisation games are great (they are), but because of how much of it they threw in the trash while making the 7th installment. I get that they at some point have to try and innovate, which is great news for civ fans, but this felt like it wasn't properly glued together. 

In short: Do not recommend in this state. UI needs to be redone to be readable, gameplay needs more variety (some interesting mechanics, like old districts or great people form Civ VI) and more optimisation. Yes, I am playing on a 8 year old CPU, but it should not stutter every second and on every menu transition on the lowest settings. Detailed review below...


1. New experimental gameplay
I like the idea of mixing and matching the leaders and empires. Does not make historic sense but makes the game more interesting (but why can you only change the empire on age transition and not the leader too?).

The ages having their different themes and little mechanics is also fun (but underwhelming, they barely matter except in the Modern age where it limits your use of Resources). But age transition "soft reset" is a good addition. It dulls the advantage of the leading empires and gives the loosing ones catch up faster.

The new Commander units bring new and refreshing battle mechanics and I would love to see them in a new Civ VI expansion.

The Towns upgrading into cities is interesting, but does not change much. The only meaningful change is that you cannot build normally in Towns, you only can buy buildings/units with gold. The Town Focus is intereting at first, until you actually look at your Towns that are not growing, not taking territory (and leaving it for your sweet neighbours), and have 4 Resources waiting just outside their border.

The Settlement Limit is a joke until you have about 4-5 cities above the threshold. It is supposed to discourage from taking or making a billion settlements, which is fine. But the game still very much relies on your production output, which IS reliant on how many settlements you have...

The Urban district mechanic (the mechanic of having 2 places for a building on 1 tile) - could be fun but it just turned out to be extremely boring. The mechanic itself is interesting, but the buildings themselves are boring. They give food or production or gold... etc. and they don't give any meaningful effects. Just: "Need more science? Take this [insert Age X science building]!". Where is the variety, the decision making which clearly was in Civ VI: "Do I build this economic district (~30 turns) to be able to buy military units in the future or should I upgrade the military district with a new building (~8 turns)?" There is no real cost difference between buildings.

And now Overbuilding.... oh man (replacing old age buildings with a new one). It would be fine if you could actually choose which building you want to replace AND if it showed the actual amount of food/productuion/science that you will loose upon destroying the previous building(s). It does not show the adjasency bonuses that you will loose which could be 2 to 3 times the amount of production/food/... from the building itself! Therefore you have no idea how much food/science/... you will actually loose, brilliant!


2. What they already had, but threw in the trash
Why aren't there any great people? Why are the Special Districts gone? Why are City-States just barbarian clans to destroy or consume as a new settlement? Why is there no climate impact, while having non stop natural disasters? Where are the brilliant ideas from previous games? They would make the game so much more dynamic and interesting!


3. The utterly unreadable UI
It looks OK, but tells you nothing. Want to check where your money goes? Too bad, it might as well be a black hole because you won't know until you click through every single city and count yourself. Want to see when did Isabella conjure up that new city? You gotta guess, because there is no history (I mean the history betwen you and the NPC's, when did they defame you, when did they form an allience with X). The tooltips on hover are here, but only for some key words. Want to change your policies, sure just click this generic looking button and then this generic looking tab. There is no personality in the UI. It looks like from a default Unreal game - fuctioning, but not functional.


4. The bugs...
There were A LOT od times where my units dealt less damage then it showed on the preview and 1 time the infantry just gave up and died without dealing damage to the city xD. Sometimes the units take a slightly different path then in the preview. The overbuilding preview calculations are just completely messed up and you should NOT trust them at all! You cannot attack an Independent power (City-State) when it is on NPC territory? It forces you to start a war with said NPC for some reason. The UI is buggy too...


5. The AI from kindergarten
It is way dumber than in Civ Vi, like night and day. I played only on standard difficulty, but it should not matter because difficulty only changes NPC buffs. Many times the enemies just made a trade route to my city while we had hostile relations to each other. An NPC with 3 cities decided to start a war with a 12 city empire, just because the relations were bad for a long time. Had 3 NPCs with 3 settlers each just wandering around, while there was plenty of space between my empire and theirs. They did see it and there was enough distance, but they just did not feel like it i guess. The overall difficulty of the game (on standard) I would rate about 2-3 difficulty tiers below standard in Civ VI. I did not have a crazy good leader or empire, just logical building and settlement taking/creating.

The economic/culture/science/... assistants are terrible too. Tried them out but quickly realised that they lack context of the game. They have the raw data but give terrible advice. Had an economic advisor propose to make a trade route to a hostile (soon to be enemy) NPC just because they had a buch of resources. And the scientific advisor told me to build some more science buildings, while I was the top science empire and about 3/4 in the Tech tree. They are great at showing the possibilities of winning scenarios, but terrible at giving advice.


6. The stuttering hell
The game stuttuers like an unoptimized Unreal Engine game. Mostly when moving the map or going throught menus. Every time you want to change what resources go to what city, stutter. I know that there are many calculations to be done, but there ARE ways to make it faster, or calculate only once every turn (and not on every window opened).


All in all it's not a terrible game, but it's not a good one either. And certailny not a great one like Civ VI. Go and play Civ VI instead. Have some fun with the Civ VI DLCs and don't waste money on this game. Unless they fix it in the future which I very much doubt, because this game has been out for over the year and most of these problems had been there from the very beginning.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game. There are a lot of things I really like about it. First, I like the return of happiness. I like that happiness is not just a result of stacking luxury resources (and I actually like how each resource has a specific bonus- at first I thought it was weird but after 1.5 play throughs I see how interesting it makes the strategy of where to settle, which tiles to improve, and where to place the resources between cities and towns). Speaking of resources, I also like that specific resources are no longer required for certain units, which really makes things more fair and less up to the random placement of this resources (no more getting unlucky with iron or aluminum, etc.). I like the return of advisers. I REALLY like the general/leader system (where the generals get upgrades, not individual units) because it basically means you never lose your unit upgrades. Units may die, but your leader usually stays around with the promotions. I like that religion seems basically the same (sending out missioners, getting bonuses for the religion, picking those bonuses). I think no faith is an improvement- just buy missionaries with gold, which means you have to balance religion with other choices in the game. I like the new diplomacy, it feels more intuitive and easier to foster friends (and foster enemies!). I actually REALLY like the ages system. I like how the first age has a cap on settlements, the rising crisis with interesting choices on how bad things get, then a return to calm and an period of new growth. It removes the whole race to settle as much as possible early on (plus happiness also restrains growth), going back to the nice balance from Civ 5 of choosing between tall and wide. I kind of like no workers (just improve tiles as the city grows- it makes city pop feel so much more meaningful and choices about where city pop goes much more meaningful). Growing cities is really fun. I do miss the busywork of assigning workers, but I think this works well instead. The narrative decisions are fun (I thought they'd be meh but they break up the pace of the game in interesting ways). I also REALLY like the multi-tiered landscape and how that influences movement and military decisions. 

Dislikes: As far I saw, there are no great works (just codexes?). I really miss assigning and trading great works and trying to get them to theme. I miss the lack of bargaining in diplomacy (you just get trades from traders). No city loyalty that I saw, which I thought was a strong perk of Civ 6. The policy screen doesn't show how yields change with different policies (tbf, Civ 6 base game doesn't do this either, but I used a mod for that so hopefully there's a mod here). BIGGEST flaw right now is that there is no single unit list that you can click on to find units. Where the heck is my auto-explore Scout?!? I don't know and have no way of finding him. Last, there's no more cultural victory? No diplomatic victory? Ages don't go through to the future era? Feels like the game is incomplete, which is not a good feeling for the base price.

I’m honestly surprised by how badly Civilization VII is being rated.

I understand some of the criticism. There are a lot of changes compared with Civilization VI, and at the beginning that can be frustrating because you naturally expect the new game to feel familiar. The Ages system, changing civilizations and some of the new mechanics take time to get used to.

But Civilization has done this before. Every major change in the series has taken some adjustment. I remember the transition from Civilization III to IV, and later the changes introduced with V and VI. At first, new mechanics can feel strange simply because they are not what we are used to.

Civ VII definitely isn't perfect, and there are things I would change, but I really don't think it deserves the level of negativity it is getting.

Once you stop trying to play it exactly like Civilization VI and start learning Civ VII as its own game, it becomes much more enjoyable. Some of the new ideas are actually very interesting, and after spending more time with them, I’ve started to appreciate what Firaxis was trying to do.

I would much rather they experiment with the formula than simply release Civilization VI again with improved graphics.

Different doesn't automatically mean bad.

For me, Civilization VII has a learning curve and needs further improvement, but it is nowhere near as bad as many of the Steam reviews make it sound.

Kudos to Firaxis for releasing a "free-week" to test the game.

Put a bunch of time into this during the free play week and while I am no longer the hater I was in the first "age" of the week, the thought that keeps coming back is "that's.. [i]interesting[/i] - I don't like it." Because now that I've spent countless hours banging my head against muddled systems and straining my eyes looking for the best bonuses, I can[b] get [/b] why they made some decisions they did, I just don't think they were good decisions.
[olist]
    [*]Keep Your Roguelite Outta My Civ (crises and age transitions)
    [*]Adjacency Autism (districts, ageless, overbuild, spacing, towns and cities)
    [*]No Trogdors Allowed (razing penalties)
    [*]City-State Your Concerns (influence, religion, other)
[/olist]
[h3] Keep Your Roguelite Outta My Civ [/h3]
Because that's what age transitions and the crises that precede them feel like to me. It's a big trial that you can't really "win" (the civilopedia says they "cannot be solved or stopped") followed by a large reset and a little bit of meta progression. I can enjoy a little roguelite now and again, and incremental games with prestige-progress mechanics do appeal to me, but I have determined these are not things I want in a 4x game. The [major] setbacks that these are should come from my opponents' actions, not core game mechanics.
For me it's not so much the lost nation perks (though there is that too), it's the lost everything. For no good reason other than I ran out of turns, everything I've been madly rushing to complete is over. Was it worth it to buy that last building that got me the final points to earn future tech, or did nothing ever matter? Yes. It feels so good to be building up your civilization in xyz aspect and moving toward your goals, and no matter how much it objectively affects you to have that progress ripped away, it FEELS awful. Again, not because [b]you[/b] made a blunder - it is not a consequence of your choices or even your opponents' - but because the game gods above you willed it.
I can see the problems ages were intended to solve, and I got a little taste of that balancing act in play. In Antiquity, I did alright. Not great, but not terrible. I was learning the game and creating inefficiencies. Focused and converted towns way too late. When the crisis came, it more or less stopped my growth and I coasted into the Exploration age. The loss was not too painful because I didn't have much to lose. But I was a powerhouse through the next one. I decided to lean into the nation change and attained numerous triumphs and future techs that led the plague to be nothing but a sneeze. I had cities, money, trade, influence and specialists going strong and in a moment it vanished. Like literally vanished. Of course I entered the Modern era well advantaged, but that wasn't the same. For a few hours there I was riding the Civ high as I watched my civilization flourish but then it instantly ground to a slog and it was like all the wind was let out of my sails. And that's how age transitions are. If you're losing, not too bad. If you're winning, they suck the life outta ya.

[h3] Adjacency Autism [/h3]
I saw someone else's review describe it using those words and thought it was a perfect description. My disenchantment with the Civ series began when they introduced districts and it has grown worse over time as they've leaned more and more into these mechanics. 7 is now the most egregious case of it. There are parts of this that will be subjective to players' preferences - fair - but objectively speaking the time sink that building cities has become runs counter to the problems the devs have tried to solve. I'm confident the majority of my time in game has been spent staring at a city instead of interacting with the world.
At the risk of sounding "back in my day", it used to be that you placed your city based solely on the yields around it. Then you built improvements and wonders all day long according to your priorities and tech. I'm not saying we should go back there, but it was [b] simple and quick [/b] and there's value in that. Complexities have been introduced to make things interesting over time and now we have yields, resources, terrain restrictions, districts, quarters, ageless, urban, rural, wonders, unique improvements, and they each have their own adjacency bonuses and interaction rules. Wonders take up a whole tile, districts HAVE to connect but you can't build through resources or mountains and the thing you know should go in that spot isn't available because it's not a city yet. But you can't go around because you want some farm/woodcutter/mine spaces for growth and once you build over them it's gone. And if you place an ageless building somewhere suboptimal for whatever reason, sorry but that's where it stays for the rest of time, future adjacencies be damned.
The point of my tirade is that there are just too many things to keep track of when it comes to planning/building a city. Nevermind what parts are/are not fun for people, the sheer quantity of them is too time consuming. To get things even approximately right, you have to spend a significant amount of time planning out each tile to maximize future bonuses and determining the route of growth improvements and district placement. Then you have to do that all over again for 15-20 cities, and AGAIN for each new age when it comes time to overbuild and place new ageless buildings. Oh but your cities are towns again and you have a bunch of other fresh starts to take care of so it'll be awhile before you can come back to that. No joke, you better take a snapshop and write down your plans because otherwise you'll come back each time asking "now what was I doing here?"
So many systems in Civ take the right amount of time. Whatever problems there may be in them, they do actually work. Exploration, combat, diplomacy, trading, research, policies, yes even pop distribution (moreso in past games) - you give it some consideration, make a few clicks, move on. Placing the next building? Hold on let me finish my calculus quick.

[h3] No Trogdors Allowed [/h3]
I was early on in one of my first games. Isabella and I were getting along and respecting each other's space. I wanted to expand closer but not so close I'd upset her. Then Ashoka goes to war with me and forward builds right between us. I defeat him and go to raze the brand new city and that's when I discover the insane new razing penalties. So I'm playing an Influence run and now you're going to kneecap my specific path because of some aggressor who made poor city placement choices? But if I decide to keep the ill-thought city, then Isabella gets mad at me for being too close to her capital. That's also when I discovered I couldn't restart the game from the esc menu because I had "already loaded a game" (why even put the button there then?!?) and was about ready to uninstall. I'm glad I didn't because I did enjoy some things, but ooh boy was that a lot of poor game design to take in up front.

[h3] City-State Your Concerns [/h3]
Look at this point any remaining issues are quibbles by comparison and I'm out of room.
City states were such a cool introduction to the series. Take them under your wing or squash them beneath your boots, the choice is yours and either way your civ stands to gain. Throw in a little competition from other civs' interests and now you're vying for control in proxy power struggles. Neat stuff. Ages really muddy the waters when it comes to their value. They were always an investment, but now through either age or being beaten to the finish line your investment is abruptly cut off with no chance of recoupment or resurgence. I just don't like the finality of it.
Plenty other problems exist, you know what they are (religion). New updates will address some and there's fun to be had, but the core game can never be made whole. They tried something and it failed spectacularly. Let's hope for a course correct in Civ 8.

TLDR: Go play just about any other Civ game
