51 hours over 1 week of FREE play; I gotta show my respect to Firaxis for the move despite the fact that I don't truly enjoy the new direction. To note, like many, been with Civ since Microprose's time and I really wanted to love Civ7.

Pros:
+ It is still Civ in a manner, I still get the one more turn urge as always (hence 51 hours lol).
+ Commander addition is fun and adds to the combat overall with leveling trees (defending chokepoint is a lot of fun).
+ Attributes and triumphs to the Civ is interesting and builds up the rush/leveling of my empire for the benefits.
+ Being able to spend influence to defend against enemy diplomatic a-hole moves are awesome for me.
+ Interesting choices of events from time to time.
+ The new change release (Test of Time update) allows me to stick with my chosen Civ till the end. My appreciation to the dev for this.

Cons:
- Age transitions are a dull and dragged/unnecessary approach... Why is my city being penalised and downgraded to town when I transition? Sure, the crisis approach has affected them but I feel that this just degrade my efforts in the previous age.
- Why is religion approach and design seems so limited now???
- Limited leaders and Civs... I know we can level up our leader/Civ to make them unique etc. but I enjoy seeing the different leaders/Civs especially when they show different personalities.
- Map is painful and annoying, I miss being able to search and find things easily; having to search wonder/village is annoying.
- Unable to expand borders barring that I spam X number of cities, is an annoying change. Realistically, there should be some ways of expanding it as it is a pain to manage/track cities especially in bigger maps. 

Summary; the latest update justify it being a proper Civ game again but there are things still lacking for an old Civ fan and I am not tempted to get this till there's a major sale with all the DLCs. I will just make do with other 4X games for now.

If you are looking for a Civilization experience that is true to the series, this will not scratch that itch. It plays much more like a Civ clone than a true Civilization game. I have been with the series ever since the very first one, back in 1992 or 93, and this is the first one that completely derails from everything I know and love in a Civilization game.

Although the game is fun at certain times, there are just way too many quirky changes from what one could acceptably expect from a game in the series. For me, the game simply isn't fun like the others.

The main disappointment is how the game was designed.

For example. the mechanic of cities/towns: You can't build stuff in your towns, you have to transform them to cities first... But then everything is much more expensive when you do... It makes zero sense, and is not even thematic. I understand they put that in there to help with late game micro management, but in my 40 hours of playing this game, by the second "era" I am micromanaging even more than, say, with Civ 6 or 5. Turns take longer, and the gains of my choices are murky at best (and yes, I understand the tradeoffs). It's like they brought 12 year-olds to design this concept. This, by itself, already makes the game not fun for me.

Another big example: The eras. Humankind came out (I have not played it) and got bashed because it supposedly does something like this, and has you switch the civilizations in between ages. I thought it could not be as bad as some reviews have described it. Well, it is definitely not fun and does not make sense either. There's no organic development of one into another. If they had done different sub-civilizations that would make up a civilization, then maybe it might be fun. But it's an utopian concept, we know that several civilizations only existed in a certain (short) periods of time. And to think that it used to be even worse, supposedly, before this last update. Now at least you can choose to keep the civilization you had on the previous age, but then a lot of all you have gets reset and you end up kind of feeling like you're having to start over. There no identity. This is not fun.

The UI is also the most confusing one that I have ever experienced in such a game. It's hard to read anything on the map. The yields screens are confusing and you really have to work your brain to try to gather all that information at once and make sense of what is going on. Complexity is not bad, don't get me wrong - but they could make it much more presentable. This is fixable, but I doubt they will do anything else here. We're already 2 years into this game.

Folks, this isn't like when Civ 5 and Civ 6 came out. They fixed those to a point where they got worthy of the name. This one isn't ever going to get fixed in the same level because some of its mechanics are fundamentally broken. There's no way to not have ages and not have cities/towns unless you completely redesign this mess from the core up.

Conclusion: A hard pass for me. I wasn't  really ever considering buying it because of all the reviews I read, and I only got to play it now because of the free week. I am certainly not going to buy it now. And to think that I got very close to preordering this game back in the day, and the only thing that kept me from doing so was the release price and little to no good stuff in the collector's edition. Am I glad I decided not to.

Looking forward, the worst thing for me is that I see there are DLCs/expansions coming out. That tells me that I will have to wait at least another 10 years for there ever to be a chance of there being a Civ 8, and even so, I will have to pray that they actually hire competent people to design and develop it.

review.review:
With Civ 5 and 6 being my most-played games on Steam, I was sent by curious friends as a canary in the coal mine to investigate the state of Civ 7 during this free week. What is the game like now after its infamous launch?

Ultimately, it feels more like a competitor game that is trying to usurp Civilization's iconic status, giving a sense that the game is competing against itself--racked with uncertainty, which is not helped by the "options" added post-launch to tone down the original vision--rather than just being a Civilization game. I felt genuinely sad, given the many cool improvements within. It's not that I was having a bad time; I just didn't feel really compelled by a "story" of my civilization relative to others.

To compare with Civ 6: the "board game"-ness has been toned down, but not removed entirely. There are adjacency bonuses, but they are harder to achieve given that city districts now must be placed adjacent to another district. While I love this change, making cities (the few true cities you will have) feel more organic, the adjacency bonuses are less impactful, so they're just kind of *there,* not feeling particularly significant like they were in 6.

The visuals contribute to a sense of liminality, between being Civilization and an upstart rival. I find the UI both atrocious and unhelpful; information is rarely available when I want it. Furthermore, geographic features have a weird scale to them. "Mountains" appear as 15m-tall rocks, and "forests" are groups of 4-5 trees. This has a big effect on what the map appears as narratively; armies in prior games could be understood as representations of larger formations, given that they were surrounded by natural features that looked imposing. Now, given that the natural features look scaled in to the unit size, my "armies" appear as a group of guys fighting for a rock on a hiking trail, as the "mountains" are no longer imposing geographic barriers but a group of rocks. At times this led to some genuine confusion; why did my unit stop moving when it got into that group of five trees? Ah, that is a "forest."

The era changes are the most controversial, and I find them still too jarring; tragic, given how baked-in they seem in the core of the game. I'm not opposed to organic civilization change; that would open up narratively significant possibilities. The era changes feel like time skips to different civilizations, rather than a real continuity from one age to the next. Given building obsolescence, automatic unit era upgrades, and the reset of most diplomacy, the last 10-20 turns of an era feel pointless. It's deeply ironic that the goal of era changes was to eliminate just clicking through to the end of the game, and now that will happen three times in a game.

There are a number of positives: privateer ships being able to attack other vessels (treasure ships and merchants!) without being at war is absolute genius and gives them a real purpose. Cities, although harder to read at a glance, do look more like cities now. I also think resources operate better than in Civ 6; the six city luxury cap always felt a little arbitrary. Now, trade is significant as your cities open up more resource slots.

I think this game could potentially shine at casual multiplayer. Unfortunately, it needs to be compelling enough for my friends to play on their own, so they can learn it; I did not really find the game to be as narratively compelling as past titles. The leader-civ disconnect and starkly changing civilizations really contributes to that, as well as civs and leaders largely feeling same-ish. Bonuses for the most part are +1 culture here or +1 science there; it never really feels like civs have unique playstyles, compared to past titles.

Truly disappointing, in the sense that there are some facets, like the military and conquest, that make me not want to go back to Civ 6. I would pick this up for maybe $15 or preferably less, just to goof around with friends.

Finally got to try Civ 7 during the free play week.

My all time favourite game franchise. More than three decades of sleepless nights building empires. Played and enjoyed every one of them since the early nineties when i got my first PC. By now i know not to judge the initial release and tend to wait for the game to mature with updates and expansions. I'm afraid any amount of maturing will not be enough with this one.

The game is over simplified and streamlined. It plays out like a console or a mobile game for an audience with a non existent attention span. No real strategy involved at any point and even the toughest choices are reduced to just A vs. B. Most of the time you just end up endlessly clicking "Next", without even needing to make a decision. Completely unnecessary micromanagement of trivial things thrown in, just to make it look like a strategy game. Most of the historical and educational value of the previous games has been completely lost.

The ages mechanic with leader and nation swapping is a truly baffling idea in a game where your main goal is to build a civilization from the ground up to stand the "test of time" (pun intended). They have tried to correct this with an update to allow you to continue as the same nation with the same leader you started with, but the hard reset between the ages is still jarring and completely unnecessary fluff.

No amount of polish, updates or DLC will ever fix this. A text book example of what happens when you let the sales department lead the project and you don't even have a clear picture of what you are trying to create. You end up releasing a half baked concept and a hurried product way too early. Littered with expensive "extra content" that really should be included in the base game. The end result is losing focus on what made your IP loved by so many of us in the first place. Trying to please everyone just ending up with a product ultimately pleasing no one. 

It feels almost like the sales execs just decided to make a final big cash out on the reputation built over the last three decades. And almost like the developers never even played or understood anything about this game series. No one honestly voiced a thought that this was not a good idea? Did all the play testers have tunnel vision? Thinking about it now, should have probably seen this coming after Civ 6.

I didn't have enough free time to buy and play this when it first came out. Noticed the initial reviews weren't very favourable and they were right. Figured it would be somehow fleshed out by now, but sadly it's not and it never will be. Sign of the times i guess, same as most entertainment in todays world. Lowering the standards to attract more buyers, only to alienate the real audience and ending up with a vapid and soulless product.

Civ was never meant to be a console or a mobile game. This version feels like one. Very sad to see a great legacy ruined. Don't see the franchise ever getting back up from this. I hope they prove me wrong.

*Played during the free week from September 7 to 11.
*My only other played game is Civ VI.


The game feels more towards metagaming then towards immersion. I can do something like trading at a higher difficultly with the gamesense I have last game and suddenly I've already snowballed hard to the point where I could nearly get the 2nd hardest victory condition for economics. Maybe I'm greedy for wanting a harder challenge while I make "great" builds and expectedly beat the AI on harder difficulties because I could put plenty of three to three to three together.

 The graphics and UI personally make it hard to evaluate and read, and the UI interactions for keyboard are confusing. Why does pressing ESC direct me back towards the menu sometimes and then sometimes work normally?

AI in this game is questionable. I could commit grievances to them, apologize in the form of cheap influence, and then they act like nothing happened? Their military decisions aren't great too. You can find them spamming cheap infantry, but they won't capitalize on taking action. They'll have two units to your one and both would willingly let you heal up first before they attack you again and then die to your fortified tile. Counterplay from the AI needs some work.

Age resets are fun. A state of going back to square one, in some balanced (and not so) state and changing gameplay is cool. Although soon its back to the "I'm number one!" state when I could jumpstart my game state imminently.

The game is obviously unfinished. They announced that they would be adding a new age, but I won't have access to the game by then. Sucks on me. The content here is dwarfed by their previous games of Civ V and VI. I would just wait until 3 years and maybe you could buy this game for cheap on a steam sale. They would have to expand further with the Civ formula and make it more complete if they want Civ VII to be a game worth playing. I appreciated my time with the game, its been refreshing to tryout a new system, but it needs fleshing.

Don't make me have to make a 2K account to play online multiplayer. Peace.

So I finally got around to playing Humankind 2, and honestly it wasn't as bad as I was expecting. Still, I wouldn't recommend buying this game in its current state. 

Pros: 
The game plays way faster than previous titles, and it makes it easier to make progress. I actually think the removal of builders/workers works fine for this installment. 

Commanders take time to get used to, but when you know how they work it makes it easier to move armies around. 

Independent Powers are great, taking the best parts of City States and Barbarians and turning them into one. They could do with some more features perhaps, but no complaints here. 

Mixed: 
Civ switching, in theory, could actually work quite well, but in its current state it feels wrong. The civ to leader dynamic feels all over the place, and many of the civ recommendations for the leaders are completely ahistoric. That's fine if you want to mix and match, but if you want the classic Civ experience, or you want a more historically accurate playthrough, staying with one civ creates an inherent disadvantage if your civ isn't in its Apex age. This one will require a lot of tinkering, but contrary to popular opinion I think this could work. Personally though, I think the necessary workaround would be to create a massive expansion pack that overhauls the game mechanics, potentially by designing each leader around four different civs, each for their appropriate age (or modifying existing civs to be multi-age). That way, it will feel less jarring to be able to have more historically accurate civs to switch to while keeping the core feel of your historical roots. 

I'm torn on diplomacy. On one hand, it creates an interesting challenge in figuring out how to spend your Diplomatic Favour, but on the other hand it ties down diplomacy to whether or not you have favour to spend. If you don't, you just can't really communicate with the others civs, ie you can't denounce them, you can't reject offers, it just feels weird. 

Cons: 
The settlement limit sucks. It just sucks. It's way too arbitrary and makes the game feel railroaded. Global Happiness despite its flaws created a more dynamic feel where as long as you keep your happiness above 0 it doesn't matter too much if you want to expand or not. With settlement limits however, you're hampered by how many cities you can build, meaning you either stick to the limit and get no penalties, or you expand and every city becomes crippled. Penalties should feel more dynamic, where if you build more cities, you receive a gradual penalty depending on how many cities you have and whether your civilization is suited to managing wide gameplay. It should vary by the type of game you're playing, not just be an arbitrary limit that prevents you from conquering and/or expanding. Takes the fun out of the game imo. The mechanic worked for Humankind because you could join cities together, but it doesn't work for civ. 

Ages... kinda suck. Not as much as people claim, but they do suck. Mainly because they feel too arbitrary and basically just reset everything, making the effort you put into building your civilization feel somewhat wasted. For example, if you don't have the dedication that lets you keep your cities, you just lose them all and have to buy more cities again. Meaning you're back to just one city again. Instead of resetting everything, why not play deeper into the crisis mechanic and make the city losses feel more natural, ie you have to fight like hell to keep your civilization alive by keeping your cities loyal through tough times, and every city that doesn't flip you get to keep. Something like that might work. So if you keep your civilization afloat, you get to keep everything, and if you lose all your cities, then it's your fault as a player instead of it being something you can't control. That would be way more fun than what we have now. 

The UI kinda sucks too. In civ 5, it felt way more natural, and information was easy to find because most of it was in one list you could click on, and there were larger buttons with inviting colours when something important needed your attention. Resources and ancient ruins were easier to identify too due to large icons, which in the case of ruins is just not a thing for some reason in this? This makes it easy to lose track of where the ruins are imo. 

The game also just isn't immersive like 5, and to some extent even 6. It feels like you're watching your leader interact with the other leaders, rather than BEING the leader. And the leader backgrounds in Civ 5 were just spectacular, it really brought the civs to life. They really should bring this back. Not to mention I'm STILL salty about them removing war music. 

Unit combat is way too oversimplified. Civ 5 had this right, where spearmen were strong against cavalry, cavalry were good against ranged units, siege units had to set up to fire, etc. I don't know what they were thinking with this change, but they really need to bring back the old combat mechanics. Every age should have 2-3 of the following: Infantry, Cavalry, Anti-Cavalry, Ranged, Siege, Naval Melee, Naval Ranged, and whatever other classes they want to add, but those ones are essential. 

Also, no Earth map. This should've been a thing since Day 1. 

In conclusion, don't buy this game until the expansion packs come. Wait and see if they make the changes necessary to fix the mistakes at launch. In its current state, the game is playable but not good. Still, it's far from doomed, and I think with a LOT of work and rebuilding the foundations from the ground up this could be a great game, maybe even the best in the franchise. But let's not get ahead of ourselves, because again, they're going to have to make some SERIOUS changes with the expansion packs if this game wants to truly feel deserving of the Civilization title.

I remember all the bad press I saw when the game launched, and that's why I was very positively surprised when I played during free week and actually enjoyed it more than both V and VI.

Pros:

You choose to subscribe to the ones relating to the victory condition you are going for and then you are only told about the systems and events relevant to the game you are playing.

Cons:

- I understand *why* they split the game into ages. It makes sense for stopping snowballs and so on. But it just feels bad when they reset so much of my hard work. I've heard a lot of bad things about Civ VII, and from what I could see in game play videos, screenshots and what the copy-cat Humankind experience was, I had zero interest in paying/playing from day one. I don't usually try the free-to-play-for-a-day crap, but was good to experience the game shortly to pass my own judgement. I've also heard other reviewers comment how they've made changes that make the game better and wanted to give it a fair trial.

It did not disappoint my expectations (which in this case were horribly low) and in good conscience I would advise people from buying this game. It is NOT Civilization. There has been some tweaks over the last year to move it closer to a Civ game and further from Humankind, but now it's just an inbred mess. Like if Sid Meiers and Amplitude had a biologically deformed child from being in a gene pool filled with games from the same family. The game takes some of the unique and best features of Humankind (like more tactical army mechanics and civilization changes through the ages) and puts it into a Civ game making these good features become terrible and mis-matched to the style of game.

2K... if I had any advice to give, it's DON'T destroy your loyal fan base over trying to match another company because your paranoid they'll take the spotlight. You did more damage than good. Remember the days post-Civilization 2 with those messy versions - Civilization: Test of Time and Civilization: Call to Power? Thankfully they tried something different and left the main title of Civilization 3 off. This is what should have been done here. This is CLEARLY not a civilization game but a try at something new Civ-esque. Changing the main era's that have been part of Civilization for 20 years to some makeshift 3 Act/Scene game that just connects three seperate era-plays together? HORRRRRRIBLE.

TO make it worse, obviously 2K has been struggling with a number of poor releases and cash-grabby marketing. They are attempting a similar form of marketing that made Paradox so rich and selling their games with hundreds of dollars in DLC. Well, newsflash. People were buying that years back but many Paradox fans have been out-priced from buying their games and this marketing method is already obsolete (maybe why they do subscriptions for their games now, also rip-offish). 2K... you're too late. Trying to make the game profitable by releasing a bunch of meaningless DLC for expansion pricing... isn't going to make up for the loss of sales on the main game. Also... adding a new leader and a civilization or two is NOT an expansion... it's a small DLC content pack. Small content packs are NOT worth expansion pricing ($30+). Stop trying to make that normal... it won't happen.

My best advice to someone watching this game. If the DLC doesn't sell, 2K will back out soon enough and scrap it. If you take a chance to buy it, and they scrap it, you'll be VERY disappointed to have a sparsely, incomplete game (Civ notoriously releases games that aren't truely complete till after several expansions... Civ V and VI, for example, didn't be come great till the two expansions later).

One other painful note. Civilization is a polished series that's had years to perfect many systems and play. This version is a horrible fail at not even including what previous Civ games had... the tracking is off (often seeing naval units move through land hexes or guys falling backwards into an ocean). There are moments of lag spikes if you take an action too quickly. The 3D models are so square and adhere to the hex boundaries that it looks 2005-ish meshes with modern textures and doesn't blend well enough to look natural. They didn't even include an option for pinning locations if you want to mark meet up points or future city sites... a feature that has been part of Civilization for many games. There are too many lost features and glitches to feel like they dropped their A-Team at Firaxis for some newer developers. Too many new changes at once and not great ones at that. A lot of poor decision making.

Best bet is wait for the flop, grab the game and DLC bundle for 90% off when they announce Civilization VIII. I bought Humnakind not to change franchises, but to try something different and I was okay with that because I didn't pay much for it. Played it a bit, appreciated the new concepts, and went back to Civ VI. I will end up buying this game too when it's $10 and probably play it when I feel like something different... but it's not worth an investment. This game is a lost cause. It's fun/intriguing but not $80+ prime Civ game fun. Now they are announcing their first PAID expansion without really fixing the game (not even sure if it's fixable; probably better off starting over with VIII).
Game is fun but way too expensive.

Before I skewer this game, I want to thank the developers for the free weekend as well as making a bunch of changes to address fan criticism. That takes courage and I respect that.

The choices you make at the beginning of Civ 5 (The one I'm most experienced in) have wide-reaching consequences 300 turns later. Civs get unique units and abilities that are relevant only at specific parts of the game to emphasise their wax and wane. Faith, Coal, and Uranium urge you to explore; Archaeology gives you glimpses of past wars on the continent you missed.
In contrast, most things in Civ 7 don't last due to how overbearing and important the age you're on is and how much gets washed away in an age transition; The past never feels like it mattered in the future.

That's not to say the game is terrible; Civilisation is never a bad game. There's things I'd love to see brought forward; I love navigable rivers and army commanders. Boats feel useful in this game when they usually don't. I like both tech mastery and the split between tech and civics. I think the crisis system is cool but isn't devastating enough and too easily ignored. I dislike the town/city split but it achieves its goal of reducing micromanagement excellently.
But the rot at the very core identity of the game, of how imposed the ages are on gameplay, means this is a good game DESPITE all of its changes, rather than because of them. I just can't recommend it when Civ 5 and 6 are right there, are cheaper and run better, and are at least the same quality.

TL;DR: I'm going to gamble that it follows the traditional arc. The pieces of a good game are here, even if it doesn't look exactly like previous CIVs exactly, and the devs seem to be making good decisions. It feels stripped down now, but so did past initial installments. Still, it's a gamble and I'm not paying >60% of full price for it.

Background:
I have been playing CIV since CIV II. I remember the long history of ugly starts followed by those first two expansions that took a CIV game from hot garbage to the new gold standard. I've seen three iterations now of "I played this, then went back to the old one which was better". I have a sneaking suspicion we're headed toward a 4th run of that cycle, especially with the new expansion and free patch announcement taking us to space.

GOOD(ish):
This CIV has some things that feel really good. City management FINALLY feels like it's something real and in-depth. Districts in VI were a good development, but also felt more like an optimization problem to place initially and flat after. VII's rural and urban centers are an interesting change of pace that actually make the cities feel like they have something to really pay attention to. The use of a soft city cap instead of a hard one made it feel less confining than I expected. Welcome back happiness! I'm happy to trade happiness for some extra land grab. Playing with towns and cities also gives optionality around how you prefer to expand, and gold purchases now feel like they're NECESSARY rather than a shortcut to dominance of the AI.  Specialist management is also interesting, since you have to lock up policy slots to really get max use out of them.

Builders are *gasp* gone. I remember being outraged when they transitioned from [x] turns to do a thing to [x] charges. Tried going back to V recently and it's literally unplayable to wait 34 turns for an improvement. Making population expansion translate to an improvement is cool and grew on me very quickly. I don't 100% know that it's going to work out, but I feel like the tradeoff of more interesting city play for removal of builders will go down as a good call. I didn't find myself missing them at all.

I love the new take on and strategy with Generals/Admirals/Air Marshalls. Way more interesting, the combat feels better, there are interesting micro decisions to make around when to scoop troops, reinforcing from afar is cool... Good call there on the CIV team. I also like that ships now are DISCOURAGED from going to the ocean in Age II but not BARRED until they magically can one day because you finish a tech. Trading damage for distance/time is a good way to let you do some exploring but also make it feel risky.

Diplomacy also feels much less painful and more straightforward now. Instead of constantly being pestered by the AI for some resource, we're negotiating pacts and treaties or insults and sanctions and that's that.

BAD(ish):
The age transition is less jarring with the Test of Time update, but there's still a feeling that your carefully built up edge that gets flattened each time. The loss of Great People and Great Works leaves a gap to some of the depth of the old games. The same interesting play around specialists that I like for added depth also creates a real pressure to lock up policy slots buffing them. 

Exploration also feels less rewarding than in the old games. I can't put my finger on why but there's just... less excitement now. Maybe because city placement isn't quite as critical? Wonders too, they don't feel quite as momentous as they did in the past. Natural wonders are pretty cool though. 

In general, the game feels smaller and less expansive than past games. I think the addition of an Atomic Age with Space gameplay will help that a lot, but that is a gamble for the future...

DEFINITELY BAD:
The monetization. Locking wonders, civilizations, everything possible behind paywalls is definitely suck. I will not be paying anything more than 60% of list on this one. I would rather pay $70 for a complete game than be nickled and dimed for 2 civs and 4 wonders every few months. CIV VI tried this too and is the first CIV game where I haven't owned all of the content, and probably won't. Treat it like a Paradox game and only buy on the sales.

CORRECTION: Great works still exist, but the interface is a little weird and I was able to play two full games without realizing where they are... That's not ideal. Great people being gone is still sad.

Played during the free weekend. If I had to sum it up, Civ VII is a game that wears the veneer of Civ but feels lacking to play in practice. Of course, at 2 hours I've barely seen what the game has to offer, but I'm not inclined to play more and it's reaffirmed criticisms I've had from watching the game.

For the good, visually the game has impressive graphics. Gwendoline Christie is a fine enough narrator, though her amount of lines (compared to Sean Bean's script in VI which also disappointed me) leaves much to be desired. The new gameplay mechanics on offer like commanders, elevation and navigable rivers also seem interesting to dig into. I especially like the independent people mechanic.

Now for the bad. Above all else, the price is egregious. The base game demands far too much, and the DLC on offer to complete the game bump it up to a staggering price. I understand that in terms of entertainment value it should make up for it, but even if I did enjoy the game, I could buy other games and be just as entertained for far cheaper. Irrespective of everything else, the price right now would always drag it down to negative to me.

Visually, the game is hard to get a handle on. Yes, it looks beautiful, but the readability makes it difficult to tell what's going on. The UI is as arcane as ever, though this would ease up with more time spent. On that note, the game has my least favorite implementation of the fog of war.

Presentation is where the game disappoints me the most. Leaders meet in front of simple banners instead of the backgrounds they had previously. Most of their response dialogue can be summed up in hmms and hahs. Civ descriptions being one paragraph long is disappointing. As someone who loves Civ V the most for its art deco style and grand presentation of history, the game that purports to show history in layers seems quite shallow considering the budget and technological advancements.

Gameplaywise, it just doesn't feel all that exciting over time. Builders being removed simplifies the strategic layer of the game to a degree I did not enjoy. Yet at the same time, I'm being bombarded with demands of what to pick and narrative event fluff. For the latter point, my agency in interpreting the world has been severely diminished. It's an experience I quite enjoy in CK2 for example, but in Civ the gameplay in this version leaves a lot to be desired. Additionally, the AI did not feel all that great here, but that's par for the course.

Lastly, having Jose Rizal but no Philippines is utterly lame. Frankly I do not like the decoupling of leaders from civilizations or the leader choice philosophy in general, but Jose Rizal was supposed to be a leader choice that resonated with me. Without the Philippines, the idea of this being the most varied Civ rings hollow, and I wish they took the time to make sure every leader has a corresponding civ.

Maybe I'll buy the game years down the line when they've improved the game even further and at a major discount, but it's a pass for me right now.

TLDR: The game feels like a sloppy mobile game with cheap dopamine hits, overabundance of insignificant choices, gameplay on rails, and some game-breakingly overpowered tactics.

Other reviews are right to be annoyed at everything resetting at each age but that criticism pales in comparison to the game's real issues (in order of significance):
	
	1. AI is horrible
	2. Overabundance of all resources
	3. Unit production cost is too cheap 
	4. Overpowered bonuses / poor power balancing 
	5. Science & culture advancement feels unimpactful
	6. Choices don't feel significant (quantity over quality)
	7. Some actions / bonuses are convoluted / not intuitive

I waited to play the game until it was free weekend to give the devs time to fix some of the glaring issues. Even though it was my first time playing I was able to beat deity level AI with mind-numbing ease on my 3rd game. Every game was a slog and frankly I was just going through the motions. I am in no way a civ expert and only have about 15 hours in the game. These are just the issues I experienced.

Issue explanations:

1. The AI which was one of the best parts of civ 6 is horrible in civ 7; constantly taking disadvantaged positions and bad fights. Even with a strong military advantage the AI will never attack you and if they did they would send like 4 units. 95% of the time the npc civs are perfectly happy just creating buildings and units making the game feel very stagnant and boring.

2-3. These issues are related and it all stems from having too much of each resource and costs being too low. By turn 10 you will have enough production to make 1 warrior per turn in the capital. This can quickly snowballs in later stages in having 20+ units at a time each requiring monotonous manual handling. Wonders are also built in ~6 turns and building them does not feel satisfying because even though they have unique bonuses you already have plenty of everything else.

4-5. In prior titles having a scientific lead would give you major power bonus over your opponent in the form of stronger units. In this game the difference between tiers of units is generally 5 strength which can be easily gapped from things like war weariness support + diplomatic actions + other social bonuses making the tiers insignificant. Even a civ with 100x your science output is easy because age progression is the same for everyone so there is no situation where you have bows and they have tanks. This leads to gameplay that feels like its on rails and never lets you fail. I appreciate devs making other ways to gain army power besides science, but the balancing is just way off. Not to mention the army and navy commanders have some new abilities in this game which lead to some very cheesy but overpowered tactics. Your archer is about to die? Just pack it with the commander and run 3 tiles with no unit collision.

6. An extension from issues 3 and 5. Each turn you make 20 decisions as to what tile to choose and which building to build, but none of these choices have any weight. 8 more production may sound like a lot but what does it matter if you already have 80 and build the strongest unit available in 1 turn? Just look through the bonuses of one civ to see what I mean about quantity over quality. Each civ gets 10 bonuses that you have to read through right at the start; talk about analysis paralysis. The kicker is you get such an abundance of resources that your civ choice likely won't matter. 

7. This issue can be alleviated with more play time, however, earlier civ titles were easier to pick up and understand

If the issues above are addressed I would love to return to this title as I am a big fan of the prior games. Most issues may be overlooked if the npc AI was a bit challenging.

Civ 7 does a few things well which I enjoyed such as tile selection on growth and resource acquisition (which eventually also turns into a slog moving resources around cities). If there wasn't an overabundance of resources it may be fun to try and optimize your output. 

Visually the game looks great but the UI looks like it’s from Civ 4. In the science screen new technologies are gold and technologies already learned are a darker gold; it's hard to differentiate the two. Some things should be clearer in the UI like the number of turns until the new age and how many turns are left on diplomatic endeavors.

At its present state the game is worse than civ 6 and even civ 5 in just about every aspect: choices with minimal strategic significance, bad AI, overabundance of resources, and a sloppy, overabundant, mind-numbing gameplay.

Though I only had time for one game during the free trial period, my first impressions are mixed. I didn't find it nearly as bad as some reviews are letting on: it's certainly different than the previous two entries, but most of the new mechanics are compelling enough for me to want to play more. Managing cities has been heavily streamlined to remove builders, which didn't bother me as much as I thought it would; you directly improve tiles in the city screen as your city grows. Combat is now focused around general and admiral units, who provide passive bonuses and can group other units together so you don't have to move them all manually, which is a welcome change. The era changes, recently overhauled in the Test of Time update, didn't bother me too much, and I enjoyed the crises near the end of each era to keep me on my toes. I liked both Civ 5 and Civ 6's visuals, and this game looks great too.

But there are also quite a few cons. Diplomacy feels pretty weak, there's no real trading or anything, just alliances. The tech and civic trees for each era feel a little boring, there are no sprawling paths, everything arranged in a diamond shape with a future tech/civic at the end. The lack of Great People is sorely missed, yet I'm guessing they'll charge money for that in a future expansion. But the biggest con for me is the UI. Everything is way too big, as though designed for a small screen, it's unintuitive and hard to find things, and never shows you enough information at a glance. Furthermore, it has absolutely no character, just serif fonts on gradients, as though it were a placeholder from an unpolished alpha version of the game. I have no idea how it was allowed to release in this state, or why it seemingly hasn't been overhauled in 1.5 years.

All in all, the game feels like an early access. I think there's a lot of promise, and maybe in a few years it'll be my go-to Civ game, but right now, large chunks of the game feel lacking or unpolished. This game is absolutely NOT worth the price, even the current sale price of 50% off, and the pricing of the DLC feels especially predatory, with expansion prices for what are essentially leader bundles with no fundamental gameplay changes. But I'm very thankful for the free trial period, so I now know this game isn't worth it yet, and to wait for a heavily-discounted bundle in a few years.

Civilization VII was a grand disappointment at launch. For a quick TLDR, I have nearly 7,000 hours on civilization V and VI. These are my two favorite games, so when I heard about Civilization VII I was immensely excited, and ready to dive into the game head first. I preordered VII like a dumby, because I thought any issues with the game at launch would be remedied through updates and DLC. This has not been the case, and I highly encourage any players debating which version of the game to purchase, to acquire V or VI and not VII. Here's why:

Pros of VII - Navigable rivers, graphics are excellent, cities' districts needing to all be taken in order to own the city, combat is better than V or VI. The aerial combat in particular is super cool, including the commander system. Commanders make the game better and are better than great generals from the previous games. Small nations are also represented better and combine a combination of barbarian clans from 6 and city states from 5.

♥♥♥♥ of VII - Main issue is the game is far too expensive for an unpolished and unfinished release. Core elements of the civilization series weren't included in the base game. The playerbase were shaken down shamelessly for more money, and I was disappointed that nations like the United Kingdom were locked behind a paywall. A paywall which also didn't include any type of game expanding features. When civilization V released DLC packs, they either included a very unique and interesting set of cultures, or a brand new game system AND new cultures. For less money. I understand inflation yadda yadda but come on! When my friends and I first played this game it crashed repeatedly during the era transitions, which were designed poorly, initially, and were often the cause of crashes. Cities in different nations look identical and it takes a good bit of squinting to see which part of the city is which. The UI is completely awful, despite what they tell you about updates, and I don't know if it can be fixed. The civilipedia is sparse, the town focuses don't show what bonuses you can receive. Cultural policies are lame and aren't permanent, meaning there is 0 sense of continuity in your empire unlike previous titles. The continuity aspect is further devastated by the era transitions on the default setting, which offer you several boring choices. You can either become a culture that is vaguely similar or related to your previous one, or you can stay the same culture and have no cool bonuses for your country.

To conclude, I was disappointed by this game. I would choose two of the previous titles over it any day. One of those titles being initially released in 2011, 15 years ago. The studio's quality is only decreasing for the almighty dollar's supremacy, and I hope the love and joy for history that was felt in the previous titles can be reinfused into either some major DLC or FREEEE overhauls for this game, or into Civilization VIII (whenever that releases I will probably have a whole new house and family.) Play civ 5 and 6, I hope this review saved you money.

I bought the settlers edition and even with that this game is so close to being just "good enough" to have a positive review but some of the cons weigh so heavy in my opinion it just kills any chances it would have had, and I really went in wanting to leave a positive review in amongst a ocean of current negative reviews even with recent updates.
I don't believe this is a worthy successor of a Civ title let alone better than Civ 6, at least in it's current state. There are many things I like and love that Civ 7 brings, and many things that it brings that I don't like and honestly make my head hurt on why the developers thought doing such a thing was a good idea for the brand.

The pros.
1. Honestly, it seems wonky at first but after some time I genuinely liked the "Grow town" or "Grow city" feature. Relying on your food production to level up essentially a settlement you own to turn a tile that your City or Town owns into a specific upgrade that could yield more resources. (Farms, Woodcutters, Clay pits and so on)
This also gets rid of the district mechanic that you'd expect from Civ 6, no longer do you need a campus district for example to build libraries (In towns you have to have the town focus set to urban center then buy the buildings)

2. I absolutely love that we can now traverse rivers in this game, both land and water units. Being able to send merchants and other trade units down rivers, and warships is honestly game changing.
In prior Civ titles I felt that unless you had coastal cities and the other A.I's had a decent amount of coastal cities to justify building naval units, It generally wasn't worth the gold maintenance and wasted time churning them out. That and unless the enemy Civs you were at war with had either a massive tech disadvantage or your ship had promotions for damage against cities and districts, it was better just to use siege weapons or a siege tower.
Now that you can traverse rivers, naval units in my opinion are actually useful now.

3. I really like the more realistic approach towards graphics instead of Civ 6s more cartoony inflated caricatures for a lack of better terms. The forests, jungles, plains and so on look very visually appeasing to the eyes, especially water tiles. The water tiles make you wish you could hop in.
I also love the small attentions to details. For example whenever you fight a hostile unit or town/city, after they've fought they continue their battle in the background for the duration of your turn. It honestly does more for immersion than you'd think and it's a great touch.
(Side note, I really love the sound track for this game involving Civ themes and ambient music.)

4. The new influence mechanic is a great new core mechanic that does wonders for any yield you have. It essentially is the diplomacy part of the game where the "Influence" is a new yield, similar to diplomatic favors in civ 6.
But instead of world congress you use it to reach certain agreements with other Civs, whether it be improve trade relations, hold festivals, boost science and culture and so on.
With some peaceful diplomacy you can really rack all your yields per turn tenfold.

5. The addition of masteries for techs and civics is great. Essentially being able to research a certain Tech/Civic twice to yield additional bonuses or abilities. Masteries aren't required to research but some techs/civics have some benefits you can't help but acquire, some might be +5 melee combat strength for all land units, or +1 Settlement limit.

The Cons
The decision to have you or other Civs play a notable historical figure for a particular nation but then have the country you play as be whatever seems to be such a pointless inconvenient mechanic to have. I feel like if they were to have kept this feature, it should have been a mode of its own in the advanced settings not a core mechanic you can't change.
I honestly have no idea why the developers thought this was a great addition, they created many additions to bring attention to detail and breathe life and immersion into the world only for them to essentially have a party game for civ selections. Seeing your lineup go along the lines of Ben Franklin of Greece, Harriet Tubman of the Majapahit, or Genghis Khan as the Mayans in the same game absolutely kills the immersion and also adds confusion with trying to decipher where people are.
The fact you can have multiple leaders of the same country in the vanilla game is wild, trying to not view "Ben Franklin" as America instead of the Khmer, then try to remember where the "actual" American player is on the map...
I feel like they could have redone this mechanic any which way and it would've been better than what we have now.

2. THIS IS SINGLE HANDEDLY THE DECIDING FACTOR on why I gave the game a negative review instead of it being a coin toss.
The fact that the game essentially ends after WW2...
You start at literally the beginnings of written history to see if your civilization will endure the test of time, only for "time" to end during the 1940s.
For almost 40 years (Civ 1 1991) the game has ended in the modern age the game was made, or the future in certain civ titles.
In my experience after this, the best way to explain the sensation of playing this game is the ending of the HBO series "The Sopranos"
You spend potentially several hours (or days) of playing as your Civ surviving thousands of years of history, all the wars, diplomatic deals, alliances, and so much more only for essentially a "Black screen and silence" once you hit the 1940s. Normally I would have left it as a small gripe, but the fact that they're selling the rest of the game as a "DLC" honestly is a slap in the face and middle finger to all loyal lifelong fans of the Sid Meier's Civilization franchise such as myself.
Normally DLCs of past entries they would introduce new mechanics and ways to spice up the game... The current "DLC" that's being worked on shouldn't even be a DLC, it should have been in the game to begin with, even the space exploration. 
The fact that they're still pushing DLC at all right now is appalling, given the criminally low reviews of the game and the fact that CIV 7 is CONSTANTLY on sale for at least 50% off because nobody wants to buy or at least try this game out.
I had a best friend of mine try this game ONCE while it was free to play this week and we didn't even get through the antiquity era before he quit and said the game is trash.

3. Settlement limits.
I can understand from a balancing perspective to prevent you or others from absolutely steam rolling the competition especially if someone spawned in a non ideal location, but the way it's implemented is very poor.
In my opinion the limit needs to be increased, not enough to completely negate its purpose but enough to not feel like you're being deliberately nerfed and held back.
Even when looking at it in the eyes of balancing, assuming you're playing on a "Earth" sized map the amount of cities/towns you're able to put down doesn't allow your civilization sprawl out nearly as big as their true life counterparts until the end of the "modern age"
Some of the Ancient and "exploration age" Civs you play as historically had more territory claimed and owned than what the game allows.

4. The age transitions, This issue also piggy backs off Con #1
I know it used to be way worse before they rolled out this past update, but it still isn't very good.
Almost all the eras of human history summed up in 3 parts.
This Con isn't nearly as big of a issue as the first 2 Cons but it's still annoying and unfortunate.

So there are certainly things to love and adore about this game, but there are also a couple of glaring "what were they thinking moments". It might get better with more development, but Firaxis should get to the drawing board on couple of items ruining the experience.
The good:
1. The early and mid game could be quite fun. There's a lot of Civ in this Civ game a lot of what has been moved from the previous games is still solid.
2. The new resource system is pretty good with two exceptions - the UI dragging is quite buggy and tedious to manage. The last era factory resources are extremely underwhelming and underpowered, especially for the required investment. 
3. The new leader tree is fun and it feels like you're creating a build.
4. The new generals are fun although I'm not entirely sure it significantly reduce the micromanagement. 
5. With the new towns/city concept gold is always useful and no matter how much you make you feel like its never enough.

The bad:
1. The era transition mechanic is just rotten to core. It's like you're starting an entirely new game each time and it diminishes what you've achieved in the previous era. It was a bad idea and bad execution. If they really want to do eras, they should take a note how Millenia was doing it.
2. The UX and UI are just "I've never played strategy game" terrible. I would call it AI slop except that AI nowadays can do a far better UI than that. 
3. Late game is just boring end turn cycling without many meaningful decisions. It's not like this problem is unique to civ7, but here the problem is more severe than most games. That's combined problem of poor balancing, AI and just the simple "number grow big" win conditions. As a result in my playthrough I spent 10 hours 1st age, 6h in 2nd age and 2h in the last age (moslty waiting for AI processing end turns).
4. The quality of leaders models and animation is on the level of 2003 3d game. 
5. Unnecessary meta progression - I know several strategy games have tried this, but it doesn't work, not in this genre when a single playthrough can take 20+ hours. Very few people play enough campaigns to make this progression in anyway meaningful.

I've played Civ since Civ Revolution on the 360. I've played Civ from middle school to college. I've read Sid Meier's book, Memoir! (the actual name of the book.) One thing that Sid stresses in the book is that when making a game, to play it until you find what is fun, and then develop that fun aspect into a larger game. Civ at its roots is a rather simple 4X game that makes it easy to get in to but just complex enough to allow for specific play styles. The fun is building up from humble roots to world domination either military or science (there are other ways to win but lets be honest, when was the last time you went for a Religious victory?(not that you can do that in this civ game))

Civ is opening a board game, seeing all the pieces and knowing you're in for a fun time. Civ 7 is not that. Civ 7 is a board game that you open, you notice all the missing pieces and promptly put back into storage in the closet, never to be touched until you either buy (DLC in this case) replacement parts to make it fun. That is not a good design nor is it anything fun. The game lacks a major amount of maps and it took them over a full year just to add real start Earth as a map, something that came with previous games on launch. 

Visually, I dislike it. I like the realism of Civ 5, I also love the somewhat more characterized look of Civ 6. This game is visually looks stunning but it lacks personality. I liked the names of rivers, seas, deserts, plains being on the map. It gave such a rewarding feeling of exploration and made venturing out feel fun and inspiring rather than just a chore to get more of the map discovered. Its a shame too, its a rather simple thing to have in the game that has a big influence on fun. 

A main issue I take with the game is that it feels half baked. Leaders can have quests (WHY) and inspiration moments that feel like its trying to have some kind of character building moments but this isn't a RPG and doesn't need those. You don't even get the full set of civs to start with. You have to play and do certain challenges to unlock more civs to play. WHY WAS THIS AN IDEA. Civ is a game that has replay-ability in its bones. "Just one more turn" has been around since the days of the first game, WHY throw in these stupid unlocks or "mementos" (boosts you can assign to start with). Its just dumb and not needed in a Civ game.

Its upsetting to get a civ game like this. Sid, in his book, champions the method of "play it until its fun, then develop that fun" when making a game. It feels like with this game, total unknowns built it and sid popped in and went "yea that looks like Civ I guess" and gave a thumbs up. I won't give him total blame for it, his name is going to be plastered on every Civ game even after his death. But he had a responsibility to make this a worthwhile contribution to the fans and he failed to realize that. Civ 6, as it stands, is the last good entry to the Civ series and any new players should start with Civ 6 or even 5.

EDIT: Deep thoughts after few more hours of thoughts and learning
I need to edit my review. My initial reaction reflected my pure disappointment right after era transition when I felt like I had lost absolutely everything. Don't get me wrong, I actually like the concept of the era transition system itself. But suddenly losing everything my civilization has learned? Hell no. Give me a choice. After analyzing it further and reading other players' thoughts, I now understand the developers' intentions and historical context. But I should still have the option to build structures from the previous era. Take that stupid bridge I have to research all over again. My civilization didn't just magically forget how to build basic bridge overnight. Give us freedom. Naturally, as science progresses, old buildings would be replaced by new ones anyway, and we’d just upgrade the existing ones. I play Civ purely as a role-playing experience, but this mechanic feels like it was designed strictly for competitive multiplayer sports. Role-play is the very soul of Civilization! The same goes for great works. Let me choose whether I want to keep them to generate  possibly tourism later, or discard them to free up slots. Or hey, let them burn down during an invasion because why not? That’s history! Here is my broken-down summary of the system after cooling down a bit:
PROS:
- Cities turning back into Towns: I actually get the concept now, and it clicked with me. Historically, some major hubs lost their relevance while others emerged, so this makes sense.
- Resource reshuffling: Having new resources replace old ones is great. Over the centuries, certain materials lost their value, which drove the foundation of new cities. Planning cities around new resources feels amazing, especially since you can build over most structures anyway.
- Crisis & Legacy system - Ending an era with a collapse or crisis feels very historically.

CONS:
- Forced "Tech Amnesia": Forgetting basic infrastructure and being locked out of building older structures completely breaks immersion. 
-Sudden peace treaty: This is a massive minus. I was literally one turn away from capturing an enemy city, and boom—automatic global peace because the era changed. That's just frustrating.
-Army reduction: While the automatic unit upgrade is a decent idea on paper, the severe army reduction feels clunky and definitely needs some fine-tuning. Why does the game automatically delete my units? Maybe I should be the one choosing which units stay and which get dissolved?- The combat itself: Honestly, the combat just isn't fun. I can't even precisely pinpoint why yet, but the actual fighting loop simply doesn't give me that "just one more turn" satisfaction. It feels tedious.

Ultimately, it’s still a thumbs down from me. I just can't properly role-play with these restrictions. I might pick it up later down the road during a major sale, but for now, it's a pass.

So why did I wait until the game was free to try it? Well... after seeing all the backlash when it came out, I was pretty much scared off and stuck with Civ 6 instead. But now that I've actually played it, I have to admit: the new mechanics really do give the game a fresh feel.

I was getting a little tired of seeing the same systems recycled with every new Civilization game, so I have to give credit to Firaxis for actually taking a risk and trying something different.

Sure, we all know how the internet works. Something changes, and suddenly it's terrible because it's not what we're used to. But honestly? I like it.

A lot of what I enjoyed about the previous games is still here, while some things have been changed or removed. And even after just three hours, I've already found plenty of new things that I really enjoy.

There are quests to complete, the military system and combat feel great, every civilization has its own distinct look, and I really like how the whole expansion system works. Tiles are upgraded immediately, and the resource system is much more interesting than it used to be.

In the older games, resources could feel pretty underwhelming. "Oh, cool. Amber. +1 Amenity."

Now resources can give you gold, culture, science, happiness, and a bunch of other bonuses, which makes them feel much more valuable. You also can't just spam 15 cities right from the start anymore. Some settlements begin as small villages that you actually have to develop and grow over time. Overall, I think these changes are a great addition to the series.

Sure, it feels a little weird when you start the game as Germany and suddenly find yourself playing as Egypt...

But here's the thing: Who's forcing you to do that? You can choose to continue playing as your current civilization into the next Age if you want. So personally, I don't really see the problem.

That said, I did run into a few things that bothered me. I was playing as the Abbasids and got dragged into a pretty brutal defensive war against Spain and another Asian faction. The fighting was intense, and I was finally getting close to winning when... Age transition.

Suddenly, every unit was back at full health and the war was over. ...What? That really killed the immersion for me. After fighting a long and brutal war, having everything suddenly reset like that felt incredibly jarring.

The camera also bugged out on me a few times, which was pretty annoying.

And then there's the thing that almost made me give up on the game before I even started: You seriously have to link the game to a 2K account, which involves scanning a QR code and getting sent to a website. Yeah... I really wasn't interested in doing that.

But whatever. I'm going back to playing the game now.

Cheers!
